六.
歪唇之客
伊萨·惠特尼——已故神学博士、圣乔治神学院院长以利亚·惠特尼之弟——耽溺鸦片成瘾。据我所知，这癖好起源于他求学时一桩愚蠢的兴起：他读了德昆西描写梦境与感官的笔墨，便把鸦片酊掺入烟草，欲求同样的效果。他与许多人一样，发现这玩意儿染上易、戒去难。多年来他便沦为药瘾之奴，亲友视之，恐惧与怜悯交杂。直到此刻我仍能见他蜷在椅中——脸黄如蜡、眼皮低垂、瞳如针孔——一位高贵之人的残骸。
一夜——是八九年六月——大约是人打第一个呵欠、瞥一眼时钟的时辰，我家门铃响了。我从椅上坐直，妻把针线活儿搁在膝上，做了个略带失望的小表情。
「来病人了！」她说，「您又得出门了。」
我呻吟了一声，因我才结束疲倦的一日。
我们听见门开，几句匆匆的话语，继而是急促的脚步踏在亚麻地毡上。我们房门猛然推开，一位身着深色衣物、戴着黑面纱的女士走了进来。
「请原谅我来得这般晚，」她开口说道；继而忽然失了自制，扑上前来，搂住我妻的颈，伏在她肩上抽泣。「噢，我陷在好大的麻烦里！」她哭道，「我太需要一点儿帮助了。」
「咦，」我妻撩起她的面纱说，「是凯特·惠特尼。凯特，你可吓了我一跳！你进来时我都不知是谁。」
「我不知该怎么办，便径直来找你了。」一向如此。陷于悲苦之人来寻我妻，正如鸟儿趋向灯塔。
「你能来，真是亲切。来，喝点葡萄酒兑水，舒舒服服坐下，把一切告诉我们。要不要我让詹姆斯先去歇着？」
「噢，不，不！我也要医生的指点和帮助呢。是关于伊萨。他已两日未归。我替他害怕得很！」
她对我们倾诉夫君的难处已不是头一回——对我是医生身份，对我妻是旧友与同窗。我们以所能想到的话语抚慰她。她可知她夫君如今何处？我们能否将他带回她身边？
看来是有可能的。她得到极确切的消息：近来每当瘾发，他便往城东最远处一家鸦片馆里去。从前他放纵不过限于一日，傍晚便抽搐颓败地归来。可如今这股魔劲已笼罩他四十八小时之久，他必躺在那码头的渣滓堆中，吞着毒烟或睡着昏沉的余劲儿。她笃信，可在上斯旺德姆巷的「金条馆」找到他。可她又能怎样？她一个年轻怯弱的女子，怎能闯进那等场所，把丈夫从围在他身边的恶汉手中拉出？
情形如此，自然只有一条出路。何不就由我送她前去？再一思：何须她去？我是伊萨·惠特尼的医师，对他自有几分影响。我独行反而办得更好。我郑重许诺：他若果在她所示的地址，我必于两小时内雇车送他回家。于是不出十分钟，我便撇下扶手椅与温馨的客厅，乘双轮马车东驰。彼时我以为这是一桩怪差，可未来才能见出它有多怪。
可我此行的头一段并无大难。上斯旺德姆巷是一条藏在伦敦桥东侧河北岸高大码头之后的肮脏小巷。在一家旧衣铺与一家杜松子酒馆之间，有一段陡峭的石阶通向一处黑黑的洞口、状若洞穴之口；我所寻的鸦片馆便藏于此。我吩咐马车候着，便走下那段被醉脚不息踩踏得中间凹陷的台阶；借着门上方一盏摇曳的油灯之光找到门闩，进入一间又长又矮的屋子——褐色的鸦片烟雾沉甸甸地弥漫，屋内有木铺成的层层卧位，宛如移民船的水手舱。

幽暗中可隐约见一具具躯体以离奇怪诞的姿势躺着——肩背弯曲、膝盖屈起、头颅后仰、下巴朝天；有几双暗淡无神的眼睛偶向新来者瞥过。黑影中闪着红色的小光圈，随金属烟斗里燃着的毒物或盛或衰而忽明忽暗。多数人静默不语；亦有人喃喃自语；亦有人以一种古怪、低沉而单调的腔调互相交谈，对话忽如喷涌而出，又忽地戛然归静——各人嘟囔着自己的心思，对邻人之言不甚理会。最里头有一只烧着炭火的小炭盆；旁边一张三脚木凳上坐着一位高瘦的老者，下巴抵在双拳之上，肘搁膝头，凝视着炉火。
我一进门，一名脸色黄惨惨的马来人侍者便忙不迭走来，递给我烟斗与一份毒料，招手让我去一处空铺位。
「不必了。我并非来留下的，」我说。「我有一位朋友在此——伊萨·惠特尼先生，我想与他说几句话。」
右侧传来一阵动静与一声惊叫。我透过幽暗细看，见惠特尼苍白憔悴、衣冠不整地朝我望来。
「我的天！是华生，」他说。他正处于令人怜悯的反应期，浑身神经皆战。「华生，我说，几点了？」
「快十一点了。」
「哪一日？」
「六月十九日，星期五。」
「天哪！我以为是星期三呢。是星期三呀。你为何要这般吓唬人？」他把脸埋进臂弯，用极尖的高音抽泣起来。
「我告诉你，今日是星期五，伙计。你妻已等了你两日。你该自惭！」
「我惭愧。可你弄混了，华生，我才在这儿待了几个钟头，三斗烟、四斗烟——我忘了几斗了。可我跟你回去。我决不能再吓凯特——可怜的小凯特。把你的手给我！你可有马车？」
「有，正候着呢。」
「那我便坐车去。可我还欠这里些账。华生，请你看看我欠多少。我神思恍惚，自己什么也办不了。」

我沿着双行铺位之间的窄道走去，屏住呼吸以避开那令人麻木的污浊毒烟，找寻掌柜。当我经过那位坐在炭盆旁的高个老者时，忽觉我的衣摆被人轻轻一拽，一个低声细语道：「走过我，再回头看我。」字字清晰落入我耳。我向下瞥去，这话只可能出自我身边那老者；可他此刻仍如先前般专注，瘦极皱极，因岁月而佝偻，一支鸦片烟斗悬在两膝之间，仿佛是从他指间因极度倦怠而滑落。我向前两步又回头一看。我用尽自制才忍住惊呼。他已转过身去，除我之外无人能见他的脸。他的身形已恢复丰满，皱纹尽消，迟钝的眼睛复燃着火。坐在炉火旁、对我惊讶咧嘴而笑的人，竟正是夏洛克·福尔摩斯。他向我略一示意要我走近；旋即他半转身回向众人时，又即刻陷入了那副颤巍巍、嘴唇松垂的痴态老相。
「福尔摩斯！」我低声道，「您究竟在这等鸦片馆里做什么？」
「越低越好，」他答道，「我耳力极佳。倘您肯赏脸把您那位醉汉朋友打发走，我将极乐意与您谈一两句话。」
「我外头有车。」
「那便请送他乘车回家。您可放心托他，看他这般绵软，怕是闯不出什么祸来。我也建议您让车夫捎一字条回您府上，告诉夫人您今夜要与我同行了。倘您肯在外头等，五分钟内我便来寻您。」

夏洛克·福尔摩斯之请极难拒绝，因其措辞总是分外明确，又带着安静的支配之风。然而我也觉得：把惠特尼安顿到车上一旦完成，我此行使命便基本告成；至于其余，我再无他求，只盼能与挚友共历他生活中那些为常态的奇异冒险之一。几分钟内我便写好字条、付清了惠特尼的账，把他送上车，目送车驶入夜色。不久，一个佝偻的身影从鸦片馆里钻出，我便与夏洛克·福尔摩斯沿街而行。两条街之间他都弯着背、踉跄而行；之后他迅速环顾，挺直了身子，爆出一阵畅笑。
「华生，我猜，」他说，「您必以为我除了打可卡因之外，又添了抽鸦片之癖——还有其他您曾以医师之见赐教于我的种种小弊端。」
「在那里见到您，我确是吃惊。」
「却不及我见到您之惊。」
「我是来寻一位朋友。」
「我是来寻一个仇敌。」
「仇敌？」
「是；我天然之敌之一——或者说，我天然之猎物。简言之，华生，我正在调查一桩极为奇特之事，盼着如从前一样，能从这些醉鬼语无伦次的呓语中拾得线索。倘我在那馆中被认出，我的命可值不了一钟头之资；因为我从前便用那馆办过自己的差事，那个开馆的奸诈印度水手发誓要找我报复。那栋楼后头、保罗码头附近有一扇活板门，能讲出无月之夜里曾从那里经过的种种怪事。」
「什么！您不会是说尸首吧？」
「正是尸首，华生。我们若就那馆里被害的每一个可怜虫各得一千英镑，便都成富人了。这是整条河岸上最污秽的杀人陷阱；恐怕内维尔·圣克莱尔进了那里便再也出不来。可我们的车驾应在此处了。」他将两根食指夹入唇间，尖利地一吹，远处即有相同的口哨回应；不一会儿便传来车轮辘辘与马蹄铿铿之声。
「华生，」福尔摩斯说，正有一辆高高的双轮单驾跑车自暗处驰来，车侧灯射出两道金黄的光锥。「您与我同行，可好？」
「若我能派上用场。」
「噢，可信赖的同伴永远派得上用场；记述者更是如此。我在『杉树邸』的房间是双床的。」
「正是；那是圣克莱尔先生的宅邸。我办这桩调查时便住在那里。」
「在哪里呢？」
「肯特郡的李城附近。我们还要驾车赶七英里。」
「我可还摸不着头绪。」
「自然。一会儿您便都明白了。请上车。好了，约翰，不需你了。这是半个克朗。明日大约十一时再来候我。让她由着她跑。再会！」

他执鞭一拂，我们便驶过了一条又一条萧瑟无人的街道。街道渐宽，最终我们飞驰过一座宽阔的栏杆桥，桥下浊水缓缓流动。彼岸又是一片砖石的暮色之野；其静寂仅被巡警那沉重而有节奏的足音、或某队迟归的酗醉之徒的歌声与喧呼所打破。一片暗云缓缓掠过天宇，云隙间偶有一两颗星黯淡闪烁。福尔摩斯沉默驾车，头垂胸前，神态如一位陷入沉思之人；我坐他身侧，既好奇这桩似如此竭尽他心力的新调查为何，又不敢打断他的思绪。我们已驶了数英里，正将到郊外别墅带的边缘时，他抖了抖身子，耸了耸肩，点燃了烟斗，神态如一位已确信自己所行最为合宜之人。
「华生，您有沉默的高贵天赋，」他说，「这使您作为同伴极为难能可贵。说真的，能有个人对话，于我是件大事——因为我自己的思绪并不愉快。我刚才在想，今夜在门口与那位可亲的小妇人相会时，我该向她说些什么。」
「您忘了我对此一无所知。」
「我们到李城之前还有恰好一段时间，我可把案情告诉您。表面看似简单可笑，然而我无从着手。线头确实多得很，可我抓不住其端。让我把案情清楚而扼要地讲给您听，华生，或许您能在这片黑暗中为我指出一星火光。」
「请讲。」

「数年前——确切而言，是一八八四年五月——一位名叫内维尔·圣克莱尔的绅士来到李城，似乎颇有钱财。他租下一座大别墅，把庭园布置得极为雅致，过得颇为体面。渐渐地他在邻里结交了朋友。一八八七年他娶了当地一位酿酒商的女儿，如今膝下有两个孩子。他无固定职业，可在数家公司里有股，照例每日上午进城，每晚乘自坎农街开出的五点十四分车回来。圣克莱尔先生今年三十七岁，习性节制，是位好丈夫、慈父，凡识他者皆喜。我须补充一句：就我们所能查到的，他眼下债务总额仅八十八英镑十先令，而他在『京县银行』账上尚有二百二十英镑的余额。故无理由认为有金钱困扰压在他心上。

「上周一，圣克莱尔先生比平日略早进城，临行时说他有两件要务待办，还要给小儿子带一盒积木回家。恰巧那同一天上午，就在他出门后不久，他妻子收到一封电报，说阿伯丁海运公司办事处有一个她久候的小包裹（价值不菲）正等她去取。如您熟悉伦敦，便知该公司办事处在弗雷斯诺街——那条街正是从今夜您找到我的上斯旺德姆巷分出的。圣克莱尔太太用过午餐便启程进城，办了些采购，前往该公司办事处取了包裹，恰于四点三十五分走在斯旺德姆巷上、正欲返回车站。我说到此，您都跟得上罢？」
「极清楚。」

「您当记得，那一日酷热异常。圣克莱尔太太走得很慢，四下张望盼能寻见马车——因这一带她不喜欢。她便如此沿着斯旺德姆巷走着，忽听得一声惊呼，抬头一望——大惊：竟是她丈夫从二楼一扇窗里俯视着她，似乎在向她招手。窗子开着，她分明看清他的脸——据她描述，那脸激动得可怕。他疯狂地向她挥着双手，旋即从窗口陡然消失，消失得那般突兀，以至于她觉得他像是被身后某种不可抗的力量拽了回去。她那女子敏锐的眼睛还瞥见一个奇异之处：他虽穿着出门时的某件深色外衣，却既无领子也无领带。

「确信他出了事，她冲下台阶——那栋屋正是今夜您找到我的鸦片馆——又穿过前屋，欲沿楼梯上一楼。可在楼梯脚她遇上了我所提的那个印度水手恶徒。他把她推回，又借助一名在那里当帮手的丹麦人，把她推到街上去了。她心中疑惧交加，沿巷狂奔，幸于弗雷斯诺街上遇见数名巡警与一位督察，正去巡逻。督察与两名警员陪她返回；尽管那馆主再三抵抗，他们仍闯进圣克莱尔先生最后被见到的那间屋。屋中无他的踪影。事实上，整层楼中除了一个相貌可怖的瘸子（似在那里安身），再无一人。那瘸子与印度水手皆口口声声起誓：当日下午前屋无别人来过。他们矢口否认得如此坚决，督察都几乎被说动，险些以为圣克莱尔太太是看错了——这时她尖叫一声，扑向桌上一只小松木盒，掀开盒盖。盒中倾出一阵儿童积木，正是他答应带回家的那件玩具。

「这一发现，加之那瘸子明显的慌乱，使督察意识到事态严重。诸屋经仔细查验，结果一切皆指向一桩可恶的罪案。前屋陈设朴素，作为客厅之用，连通一间小卧室；卧室窗朝着某座码头之背面。码头与卧室窗之间有一窄条之地：低潮时干燥，高潮时则被至少四英尺半深的水所淹没。卧室窗宽阔，从下方推开。一查：窗台上有血迹，卧室木地板上也有数滴散落。前屋窗帘后藏着内维尔·圣克莱尔先生的全部衣物——除外套之外。靴子、袜子、礼帽、表——皆在。这些衣物上无暴力痕迹，亦再无内维尔·圣克莱尔先生的踪影。除了从窗口出去之外，似别无他出口；窗台上那些不祥的血迹也使他难有泅水自救的指望——因为惨剧发生时正是潮水最高之刻。
「至于那两名似乎与此事直接相涉的恶人。那印度水手据说有最污秽的过往；可按圣克莱尔太太所述：她丈夫现身窗口后数秒钟内，他便已在楼梯脚——这就难以使他比一名从犯更甚。他以全然无知作为辩词，又抗辩道：对其房客休·布恩之所行所为他一概不知，对失踪绅士之衣物何以在此屋中亦无从解释。

「印度水手掌柜的事便如此。再说那住于鸦片馆二楼之上、相貌阴森的瘸子——他无疑是最后一个目睹内维尔·圣克莱尔的人。他名叫休·布恩；其丑陋之相，凡常去伦敦城中之人无不熟悉。他是一名职业乞丐——为避警章，他假托做小本生意卖蜡火柴。在针线街向左略下，您兴许留意过墙上有处小小的内拐角；这家伙便每日盘腿坐于此，膝上摆着小小的火柴存货——他其貌堪怜，故有一阵阵小小的施舍如雨般落入他身侧人行道上的那顶油腻皮帽里。早在我尚未起意要与他这一行打交道之前，我便不止一次留意过他；并惊叹于他短时间内之收获。您看，他相貌如此非凡，没人能从他身边路过而不留意。一头乱蓬蓬的橘色头发，一张被一道可怖伤痕扭曲了的苍白脸——那伤痕因收缩而把上唇外缘翘起，露出三颗牙齿——一只斗牛犬般的下巴，一双极为透人的深色眼眸——眼眸的颜色与他的发色形成奇特的对照——这一切都令他在乞丐之群中显得卓然不群。他的机锋亦然——路人但凡掷一句戏言，他必有妙答。这便是我们如今得知的——曾在那鸦片馆寄宿、最后见过我们所寻之绅士的人。」
「可他是个瘸子！」我说。「他孤身一人怎能对付得了一位风华正茂的男子？」
「他瘸不过是说他走路一瘸一拐；其他方面，他似乎是位强壮且营养良好的男子。华生，您的医道经验当能告诉您：一肢之弱往往可以靠它肢之卓异之力来弥补。」
「请继续讲。」

「圣克莱尔太太一见窗上血迹便晕了过去，警方将她乘车送回家中，因她在场对调查无益。负责本案的巴顿督察对屋舍进行了极仔细的查验，可未发现任何能为案情指明线索之物。当时犯了一个错——未即刻逮捕布恩，使他得着几分钟时间，或可与他朋友——那印度水手——通了气；可此误不久即得弥补。他被擒、被搜，搜不出任何能罪证他之物。诚然，他右衫袖上有几点血迹；可他指着自己食指——指上靠近指甲处有伤口——解释血来自此。他还说他不久前去过窗口，窗上所见血迹想必亦同源。他坚决否认见过内维尔·圣克莱尔先生，并发誓他屋内出现衣物对他来说与对警方来说同样是个谜。至于圣克莱尔太太说她确曾见到丈夫在窗口一节——他声言她必是疯了或在梦中。他被押入警局，一路高声抗辩；督察则留在原处，盼退潮或可提供新线索。
「果然——只是他们在泥滩上所发现的，并非他们所惧怕的那一物。是内维尔·圣克莱尔的外套，并非内维尔·圣克莱尔本人——那外套随潮水退去而显露。您猜他们在口袋里发现了什么？」
「我猜不到。」
「不，我看您也猜不到。每一个口袋都塞满了便士与半便士——四百二十一枚便士与二百七十枚半便士。难怪潮水未把它带走。可人之尸首便另当别论了。码头与屋舍之间有一道猛烈的回流，料想衣物因负重而留下时，赤身的尸首已被吸入河中。」
「可我所知，其他衣物都已在屋中寻得。难道尸首会只穿一件外套？」

「不，先生，但事实可被说得头头是道。设想这位布恩把内维尔·圣克莱尔从窗推了出去——这一行无人可见。他将如何应对？立时他必想到要除去会暴露之物。他抓起外套，正欲掷出窗外，又忽想：它会浮而不沉。时间紧迫——他听见楼下夫人欲强闯而上时的扭打声；或许他已从他的印度水手同伙处听说警察正涌上街来。一刻不容耽误。他奔向某处秘藏——他乞讨所得之果——把手所能触的一切硬币都塞入袋中以确保外套之沉。他扔了出去；本欲也将其余衣物如此处置，可此时听到楼下脚步如潮涌至，他只来得及关上窗户，警察便至。」
「这听起来确有可行之处。」
「好罢，我们暂且把它当作一个工作假设——别无更好的可代之。布恩，如我所言，被捕押入警局。可亦无法证明此前他曾有任何可疑之举。他多年以来一直被人知作职业乞丐；他生平似甚为安静与无辜。事情眼下便至此地步——而须解开的疑问——内维尔·圣克莱尔在鸦片馆里做什么？在那里他遭遇了什么？如今他在何处？休·布恩与他失踪何关？——皆遥遥无解。我承认，我所历的案中尚无一桩，乍看如此简单，竟有如此之难。」
夏洛克·福尔摩斯把这一连串奇异事件细述时，我们已穿过这座大都市的郊外，零星房屋皆抛在身后；我们沿着两侧皆为乡间篱笆的路辘辘前行。他叙完时，我们正驶过两个零落的小村，几扇窗里仍闪着零星灯火。
「我们已到李城郊外，」我同伴道。「这短短的车程内，我们已掠过英格兰三个郡——自米德尔塞克斯起，越过萨里之一角，终于肯特。瞧那林间一星灯——便是『杉树邸』；那灯旁坐着一位夫人——她那焦虑的耳朵想必早已捕捉到我们马蹄之声了，我可不怀疑。」
「可您为何不在贝克街办这案子？」我问。
「因为有许多查询须在此处进行。圣克莱尔太太极慷慨地为我安排了两间客房，您可放心，对我的朋友兼同事她除了欢迎别无他言。华生，每当我无她夫君的消息便要去见她，于我极为难堪。到了。咴，咴！」
我们在一座大别墅前勒马停下，那别墅自有庭园。一名马童奔出来牵马；我跳下车，随福尔摩斯走上那条蜿蜒的小碎石车道，引向宅邸。我们走近时，门陡然敞开，一位个子娇小的金发女子立于门洞之中。她身着一袭轻薄的真丝薄纱，颈间与腕上点缀着粉色雪纺。她的身影逆光而立——一手扶门，一手急切地半抬，身子微倾，头与脸前探，眼神热切，唇微张——便是一个站立的疑问。
「如何？」她叫道，「如何？」继而她见来者是两人，发出一声希望的呼喊，又见我同伴摇头耸肩，那希望便化作一声呻吟。
「无好消息？」
「也无坏消息？」
「谢天谢地。请进。两位想必已疲惫了，跑了一日的长路。」
「这是我朋友华生医生。他在我多桩案子里皆助我极大。今夜机缘巧合，我得以将他带来与我同办这桩调查。」
「能见到您，我非常欢喜，」她热切地握住我的手说道。「我相信您会原谅我们陈设上的种种欠周——若您体谅这场如此突然降临的打击。」
「我亲爱的女士，」我说，「我是个老兵，纵然不是，我也明白此处无须任何道歉。倘我能为您或为我此处的朋友尽一点力，便已是我莫大的欣幸。」
「夏洛克·福尔摩斯先生，」我们走入一间灯火明亮的餐厅时这位夫人说道——桌上已摆好冷食晚餐——「我极想问您一两个直白的问题，恳请您直白作答。」
「自然，夫人。」
「不必顾及我的感受。我并非歇斯底里之人，亦不易晕厥。我只想听您真实、真实的看法。」
「就哪一点？」
「内心深处，您觉得内维尔还活着么？」
夏洛克·福尔摩斯似为此问所窘。「请直言！」她重复，立在地毯上，敏锐地俯视那靠在藤椅中的他。
「直言罢，夫人，我以为他不在了。」
「您以为他已死？」
「正是。」
「被害？」
「这我未敢言定。或许。」
「他是哪一日身死的？」
「星期一。」
「那么，福尔摩斯先生，请您解释解释：今日我何以收到他寄来的一封信？」
夏洛克·福尔摩斯如被通了电般从椅上跃起。
「什么！」他大吼。
「是的，今日。」她微笑而立，举起一片小小的纸条。
「容我一观？」
「自然。」
他急切地从她手中抢过来，摊在桌上，又把灯拉过来，凝神细察。我离了座，伏在他肩后端详。信封极粗劣，盖着格雷夫森德的邮戳，日期便是当日——更确切是前一日，因如今已过半夜许久。
「字迹粗劣，」福尔摩斯喃喃道。「夫人，这必非您夫君的笔迹。」
「不是，可信中所附是。」
「我亦看出，写信封之人须先去打听地址。」
「您是怎么看出的？」
「您看，姓名是用纯黑墨水写的，已自行干透；其余则是淡灰色——这表明用了吸墨纸。倘是一气呵成再吸墨，便不会有任何处呈深黑。此人先写下姓名，写地址前停顿了一会儿——这只能意味着他对地址不熟悉。这自然是琐细之事，可再没什么比琐细之事更要紧的了。如今让我们看信。哈！这里附有别物！」
「是，曾有一枚戒指——他的图章戒。」
「您确信这是您夫君之手笔么？」
「是他的『一手』。」
「他匆忙时所写的那一手。与他平日手书极不相似，可我熟悉得很。」
「『至爱：莫怕。一切将好。其中一桩大错或须些时日方能厘清。耐心等我。——内维尔。』以铅笔写于一本八开本书的扉页上，无水印。嗯！今日由格雷夫森德某位手指肮脏的人投寄。哈！如我没看错，封口处之胶是由一位嚼烟草之人粘上的。夫人，这是您夫君之手笔无疑？」
「无疑。这字句正是内维尔写的。」
「且今日由格雷夫森德投寄。圣克莱尔太太，乌云已有所明朗，虽然我尚不敢断言危险已过。」
「可他必还活着，福尔摩斯先生。」
「除非这是巧妙的伪造，意在把我们引上歧路。戒指其实并不能证明什么，它可能是从他身上取去的。」
「不，不；这是、是他自己的笔迹！」
「极好。然而它亦可能是星期一所写，今日才投寄。」
「这有可能。」
「若如此，其间或已发生很多事。」
「噢，请勿教我灰心，福尔摩斯先生。我知道他一切平安。我们之间的感应何等敏锐——如有不测降于他，我必觉之。我最后一次见他那一日，他在卧室里割伤了自己；可我在餐厅里立时奔上楼来，万分确信发生了什么。您以为我会对那般小事有所感应、却不知他之身亡么？」
「我所阅多矣，深知妇人之直觉有时比一位分析推理者的结论更为可贵。在这封信中，您确实掌有强力之证据足以印证您之看法。可若您夫君尚在人世且能写信，他何以远离您？」
「我无从想象。这不可思议。」
「星期一他离您之前可曾留下何言？」
「您在斯旺德姆巷见他时也很惊讶？」
「极为惊讶。」
「窗子是开着的么？」
「那他便可能呼唤您？」
「他可能。」
「可据我所知，他只发出一声不成语之喊？」
「您当是以为是求救之喊？」
「是。他还挥着手。」
「但那也可能是惊喊。意外见到您，惊讶之下他或会扬起双手？」
「这有可能。」
「您以为他被人拽了回去？」
「他消失得太突然了。」
「他亦可能自行往后一跃。屋中您可见到别人？」
「未。可那个可怕之人承认当时在场，那印度水手则在楼梯脚。」
「正是。就您所能见到的，您夫君穿着平日的衣物？」
「但无领子也无领带。我分明看见他赤裸的喉。」
「他可曾提起过斯旺德姆巷？」
「从未。」
「他可曾露出任何抽鸦片的迹象？」
「从未。」
「多谢您，圣克莱尔太太。这便是我所欲彻底厘清的几个要点。我们这就稍用一点晚餐再去歇息——明日我们或将极忙。」

我们获得了一间宽大舒适的双床房。我经此一夜的奇遇已疲倦至极，很快便钻入了被窝。然而夏洛克·福尔摩斯素来如此：心头一旦有未解之难题，他便能数日甚或一周不息——翻来覆去、重整事实、自每一角度审视，直至或洞悉案情，或确信资料不足。我不久便察觉，他正准备彻夜枯坐。他脱去外套与背心，套上一件宽大的蓝色睡袍，便在屋里来回踱步，从他床上拢来枕头，又从沙发与扶手椅上拢来坐垫。他用这些堆成了一种东方式的小榻，盘腿坐于其上，前面摆好一盎司散叶烟与一盒火柴。在灯火幽暗中，我看见他坐在那里——一支老旧的欧石南木烟斗叼在唇间，眼神空洞地凝着天花板的一角，蓝色烟雾自他袅袅升起；沉默不动，灯光照在他刚毅的鹰隼般侧影上。我入睡时他便如此坐着；待我被一声忽然的惊叫唤醒，发现夏日朝阳已照入屋内，他仍如此坐着。烟斗仍叼在唇间，烟雾仍向上升腾，屋内浓密的烟雾弥漫，可我前夜所见的那一堆散叶烟已无所剩。
「醒了么，华生？」他问。
「醒了。」
「可有兴致与我一同晨驾？」
「自然。」
「那便穿衣。眼下尚无人起身，可我知道那马童睡在何处，我们不久便能把车备好。」他说着自顾咯咯笑起来，眼中含光，与昨夜那位阴郁的思考者俨然两人。
我穿衣时瞥了一眼怀表。无怪乎尚无人起身——才四点二十五分。我才更衣完毕，福尔摩斯便回来报告说马童正在套马。
「我想检验我的一个小理论，」他一面穿靴一面说。「华生，我看您此刻正立于全欧洲最绝顶的傻瓜之一面前。我该被人从此处一脚踢到查令十字。可我想，眼下我已掌握此案的钥匙了。」
「钥匙在哪里呢？」我笑着问。
「在浴室里，」他答道。「噢，是的，我并非开玩笑，」他见我神色狐疑，便接着说。「我刚才便在那里，已把它取了出来，装在这只格莱斯顿包里。来吧，我的小子，看它是否能与那把锁相合。」
我们尽量轻声地下了楼，走入晨光朗照之中。路上停着我们的马与马车，那衣衫不整的马童正在马首旁候着。我们俩跃身上车，沿伦敦路飞驰而去。几辆乡间运货车开始动了，载着蔬菜进京；可两侧那一排排别墅却如梦中之城般静寂无生。
「这案子在某些方面颇为奇异，」福尔摩斯一鞭催马至飞奔。「我承认我盲如鼹鼠；可晚学得智慧总胜于全然不学。」
我们驶过萨里这一侧街道时，城中最早起者刚开始睡眼惺忪地从窗内望出。我们顺滑铁卢桥路而下，过了河，从惠灵顿街疾驰而上，向右一急转便到了弓街。夏洛克·福尔摩斯于此处警力中已颇有名望，门口两名巡警向他敬礼。一名牵着马首，另一名领我们入内。
「谁当值？」福尔摩斯问。
「布雷德斯特里特督察，先生。」
「啊，布雷德斯特里特，您好？」一位高大壮实的官员沿石板廊道走来，戴尖顶帽，穿绣线扣短上衣。「布雷德斯特里特，我想与您悄悄说一句。」
「自然，福尔摩斯先生。请进我屋里。」
那是一间小小的、办公室般的房间，桌上有一本巨大的账簿，墙上嵌着电话机。督察坐到办公桌前。
「能为您效什么力，福尔摩斯先生？」
「我来问那个乞丐布恩——便是被指控与李城内维尔·圣克莱尔先生失踪一案有涉的那人。」
「是。他已被押上来过、又因待续调查而被还押。」
「我所闻。他在此处？」
「在牢房里。」
「他可安静？」
「噢，他不惹事。可他是个肮脏的恶棍。」
「肮脏？」
「是，让他洗手都得费九牛二虎之力，他的脸黑得像锅炉匠的脸。等他这案子断了，他必得受一次正经的牢狱沐浴；倘您见到他，必会与我同感他需要一洗。」
「我极想见他一面。」
「您想？这易如反掌。这边请。您那只包可放下。」
「不，我想我还是带着。」
「极好。请这边走。」他领我们沿一条廊道而下，开了一道铁条门，又走下一段蜿蜒的楼梯，把我们带到一条粉刷成白色的过道——两侧成排是牢门。
「右起第三便是他的，」督察说。「就这里！」他轻轻拉开门顶部的小窥板，向内一望。
「他在睡觉，」他说。「您可看得清楚。」
我们俩把眼贴上铁栅。囚徒面朝我们躺着，沉睡极深，呼吸缓重。他是个中等身材的男子，衣着粗陋——与他这一行相称——破烂的外套裂口里露出一件彩色衬衫。如督察所言，他极脏；可那覆面之尘垢仍掩不住其相之丑陋。一道宽宽的旧疤痕自眼至下巴横贯其面，因疤痕之收缩而把上唇一侧翘起，露出三颗牙齿，呈出一种永不消散的咧嘴讥笑。一头极鲜亮的红发低低生在他眼与额之上。
「他真是个『美人儿』，是不？」督察道。
「他的确需要一洗，」福尔摩斯说。「我猜想他可能需要，便擅自带了工具来。」他说着打开格莱斯顿包，令我大惊的是，竟取出一块极大的浴用海绵。
「呵！呵！您真是个有趣之人，」督察咯咯笑道。
「请劳您之驾，极轻地把那扇门打开，我们不久便能让他换上一副远为体面的相貌。」
「好罢，倒不知有何不可，」督察说。「他这副模样可不光彩弓街的牢房，是不？」他把钥匙插入锁孔，我们便都极轻地走入囚室。睡者半翻了个身，又复沉沉睡去。福尔摩斯俯身向水罐，浸湿海绵，便在那囚徒脸上有力地横擦、竖擦了两下。
「容我向诸位介绍，」他大声道，「肯特郡李城的内维尔·圣克莱尔先生。」
我此生从未见过这般景象。那人的脸在海绵之下脱落，宛如树皮自树身脱落。粗劣的褐色去了！横贯其面的丑陋伤痕去了，那令脸庞带上厌恶讥笑的歪唇也去了！轻轻一抹，那一团乱蓬的红发亦被取下；坐在床上揉着眼睛、睡眼惺忪地四下张望的，是一位面色苍白、神情忧愁、举止文雅的男子，黑发洁肤。继而他骤然意识到自己已被揭穿，便发出一声尖叫，扑下脸贴向枕头。
「天哪！」督察叫道，「这果然便是失踪之人，我能从相片上认出他来。」
囚徒以一种听天由命的鲁莽神态翻过身来。「便如此罢，」他说。「请问我被指控何罪？」
「指控您害死内维尔·圣克莱尔——噢，得了，您可不能被指控这个，除非他们以企图自害立案，」督察咧嘴笑道。「我在警队二十七年，这事真是头一遭。」
「倘若我便是内维尔·圣克莱尔先生，则显然无罪可言；故我系被非法拘留。」
「无罪，可一桩极大的错误已被铸就，」福尔摩斯说。「您本应信赖您的夫人。」
「不是夫人——是孩子，」囚徒呻吟道。「上苍助我，我可不愿让他们因父亲而蒙羞。我的天！这般张扬！我又能怎么办？」
夏洛克·福尔摩斯在长榻上紧挨他坐下，亲切地拍了拍他的肩。
「倘您把此事交由法庭来澄清，」他说，「自然难免公之于众。反之，倘您能让警务当局确信对您实无可立之案，我看其细节倒未必非要见诸报端不可。布雷德斯特里特督察必能就您所告之事作笔录，呈递相关部门。如此则此案根本无须上庭。」
「上苍保佑您！」囚徒激动地叫道。「我宁愿入狱、宁愿赴刑，也不愿把这桩可悲的秘密留作家族污点遗给我的孩子。

「您是头一个听我故事之人。我父亲是切斯特菲尔德的一位塾师，我在那里受了极好的教育。年轻时我四处游历，曾入舞台之业，最后成了伦敦一家晚报的记者。一日，我的编辑想做一系列关于京城乞讨的报道，我自告奋勇供稿。我所有的奇遇便由此发端。要写这些文章，唯一办法便是亲自体验乞讨。我做过演员，自然学得了一切化装的秘诀，在后台以此技闻名。我便用上了所学。我在脸上绘了妆，又为令自身尽量可怜，做了一道好看的伤痕，并以一小块肉色橡皮膏把上唇一侧固定为歪扭之状。然后戴上一头红发，配以相应的衣装，便在城内商业区当街设下我的摊位——表面上是卖火柴，实则乞讨。我一连干了七小时，傍晚归家时大惊：我所获不下二十六先令四便士。
「我写完文章便没再多想此事；过了一阵我替朋友作保，被一张二十五英镑的支票传票送上门来。我不知这钱从何处筹得；忽生一计：我向债主求两周宽限，向雇主请假，便穿上化装在城里乞讨。十日内我便挣得这笔钱，把债清了。

「您可以想见，我已知我每日只须在脸上抹一点颜料、把帽子放在地上、坐在那里不动便能挣得一日所得，要我还安心做每周二英镑的辛苦工是何等难。我自尊与金钱之间斗争甚久，最终还是金钱赢了。我便辞了报馆的差事，日复一日坐在我最初选定的那处街角，靠那张可怖的脸博取怜悯，把口袋装满铜币。只一人知我之秘，便是我从前在斯旺德姆巷某下等馆寄宿——那处掌柜。每日清晨，我可化作一个污秽的乞丐而出；每晚则在那里变身为一位衣装齐整的城中绅士。这家伙是个印度水手，房费我付得他甚厚，我便知我之秘在他手中无虞。
「不久我便发现自己存下了相当可观的款项。我并非说伦敦街头随便哪个乞丐都能挣到一年七百英镑——这还低于我之平均所得——可我在化装一术上又有奇能，且口才便给——经过练习愈见出色，使我在城中颇有名气。一整日里铜币如流，间或有银币，落入我手；要逢一日挣不到二英镑，便算是极坏的一日了。
「我愈富便愈有抱负，便在乡间买下宅邸，最终成婚——无人对我真正的差事有所怀疑。我的爱妻只知道我在城中有事。她哪知是何事。

「上周一我已歇工，正在鸦片馆楼上自己的房中更衣，望出窗外——令我惊恐又惊愕——我妻竟立在街上，目光直直注视着我。我惊呼一声，扬起双手遮面；冲到我的知交那印度水手前，恳他阻止任何人上来。我听见她在楼下的声音，可知她上不来。我迅速脱去衣物，套上乞丐的衣裳，敷上颜料、戴上发套。便是妻子之眼亦穿不破这般完整的伪装。可此时我又想到屋中或将被搜，那些衣物或将出卖我。我一把推开窗子——这一暴力之举把我那日清晨在卧室内自伤的小口子又裂了开来。然后我抓起外套——那外套因我刚把皮袋中所收之硬币转入其中而沉甸甸的——把它甩出窗外，外套便消失于泰晤士河中。其余衣物本欲跟着扔出，可此时楼梯上巡警之声如潮涌至，几分钟后我发现——说实话，倒令我松了口气——我竟非被认出为内维尔·圣克莱尔先生，而是被作为他的杀人凶手而捕。
「再无别的可向您解释了。我决意尽可能久地保持化装，故宁愿带着一张污脏之脸。我也知妻必焦灼难安，趁巡警未注视我之时，便取下我的戒指，连一张匆匆潦草写就的字条一同托付那印度水手——告诉她她无须忧惧。」
「那张字条到她手中是昨日的事，」福尔摩斯说。
「我的天！她这一周必如何度过！」
「警方一直在监视那印度水手，」布雷德斯特里特督察说，「我可以理解，他要在不被察觉时把信寄出确有难处。想必他把信交给了某位水手主顾，那人却把这事忘在脑后好几日。」
「正是如此，」福尔摩斯赞许地点头。「这点我毫不怀疑。但您从未因乞讨被起诉么？」
「数次；可一笔罚款于我何足道哉？」
「然而这一切必须在此终止，」布雷德斯特里特说。「警方若要把此事压下，便决不能再有什么休·布恩了。」
「我已以人间所能立的最庄严的誓言起誓。」
「如此则估计可不必再有进一步处置。可您若再被发现，则必须一切公之于众。福尔摩斯先生，敝署对您能为我们厘清此事十分感激。我倒愿知您是怎么得出您的结论的。」
「这一桩，」我朋友说，「我是凭着坐在五只枕头之上、抽掉一盎司散叶烟而得出的。华生，我想我们若驾车回贝克街，正好赶得上吃早餐。」

11.title: XI. THE ADVENTURE OF THE BERYL CORONET
source_paragraphs:
XI.
THE ADVENTURE OF THE BERYL CORONET

“Holmes,”
said I as I stood one morning in our bow-window looking down the street,
“here is a madman coming along. It seems rather sad that his relatives
should allow him to come out alone.”

My friend rose lazily from his armchair and stood with his hands in the pockets
of his dressing-gown, looking over my shoulder. It was a bright, crisp February
morning, and the snow of the day before still lay deep upon the ground,
shimmering brightly in the wintry sun. Down the centre of Baker Street it had
been ploughed into a brown crumbly band by the traffic, but at either side and
on the heaped-up edges of the footpaths it still lay as white as when it fell.
The grey pavement had been cleaned and scraped, but was still dangerously
slippery, so that there were fewer passengers than usual. Indeed, from the
direction of the Metropolitan Station no one was coming save the single
gentleman whose eccentric conduct had drawn my attention.

He was a man of about fifty, tall, portly, and imposing, with a massive,
strongly marked face and a commanding figure. He was dressed in a sombre yet
rich style, in black frock-coat, shining hat, neat brown gaiters, and well-cut
pearl-grey trousers. Yet his actions were in absurd contrast to the dignity of
his dress and features, for he was running hard, with occasional little
springs, such as a weary man gives who is little accustomed to set any tax upon
his legs. As he ran he jerked his hands up and down, waggled his head, and
writhed his face into the most extraordinary contortions.

“What on earth can be the matter with him?” I asked. “He is
looking up at the numbers of the houses.”
“I believe that he is coming here,” said Holmes, rubbing his hands.
“Here?”

“Yes; I rather think he is coming to consult me professionally. I think
that I recognise the symptoms. Ha! did I not tell you?” As he spoke, the
man, puffing and blowing, rushed at our door and pulled at our bell until the
whole house resounded with the clanging.

A few moments later he was in our room, still puffing, still gesticulating, but
with so fixed a look of grief and despair in his eyes that our smiles were
turned in an instant to horror and pity. For a while he could not get his words
out, but swayed his body and plucked at his hair like one who has been driven
to the extreme limits of his reason. Then, suddenly springing to his feet, he
beat his head against the wall with such force that we both rushed upon him and
tore him away to the centre of the room. Sherlock Holmes pushed him down into
the easy-chair and, sitting beside him, patted his hand and chatted with him in
the easy, soothing tones which he knew so well how to employ.

“You have come to me to tell your story, have you not?” said he.
“You are fatigued with your haste. Pray wait until you have recovered
yourself, and then I shall be most happy to look into any little problem which
you may submit to me.”

The man sat for a minute or more with a heaving chest, fighting against his
emotion. Then he passed his handkerchief over his brow, set his lips tight, and
turned his face towards us.
“No doubt you think me mad?” said he.
“I see that you have had some great trouble,” responded Holmes.

“God knows I have!—a trouble which is enough to unseat my reason,
so sudden and so terrible is it. Public disgrace I might have faced, although I
am a man whose character has never yet borne a stain. Private affliction also
is the lot of every man; but the two coming together, and in so frightful a
form, have been enough to shake my very soul. Besides, it is not I alone. The
very noblest in the land may suffer unless some way be found out of this
horrible affair.”

“Pray compose yourself, sir,” said Holmes, “and let me have a
clear account of who you are and what it is that has befallen you.”

“My name,” answered our visitor, “is probably familiar to
your ears. I am Alexander Holder, of the banking firm of Holder &
Stevenson, of Threadneedle Street.”

The name was indeed well known to us as belonging to the senior partner in the
second largest private banking concern in the City of London. What could have
happened, then, to bring one of the foremost citizens of London to this most
pitiable pass? We waited, all curiosity, until with another effort he braced
himself to tell his story.

“I feel that time is of value,” said he; “that is why I
hastened here when the police inspector suggested that I should secure your
co-operation. I came to Baker Street by the Underground and hurried from there
on foot, for the cabs go slowly through this snow. That is why I was so out of
breath, for I am a man who takes very little exercise. I feel better now, and I
will put the facts before you as shortly and yet as clearly as I can.

“It is, of course, well known to you that in a successful banking
business as much depends upon our being able to find remunerative investments
for our funds as upon our increasing our connection and the number of our
depositors. One of our most lucrative means of laying out money is in the shape
of loans, where the security is unimpeachable. We have done a good deal in this
direction during the last few years, and there are many noble families to whom
we have advanced large sums upon the security of their pictures, libraries, or
plate.

“Yesterday morning I was seated in my office at the bank when a card was
brought in to me by one of the clerks. I started when I saw the name, for it
was that of none other than—well, perhaps even to you I had better say no
more than that it was a name which is a household word all over the
earth—one of the highest, noblest, most exalted names in England. I was
overwhelmed by the honour and attempted, when he entered, to say so, but he
plunged at once into business with the air of a man who wishes to hurry quickly
through a disagreeable task.

“‘Mr. Holder,’ said he, ‘I have been informed
that you are in the habit of advancing money.’

“‘The firm does so when the security is good.’ I
answered.

“‘It is absolutely essential to me,’ said he, ‘that I
should have £ 50,000 at once. I could, of course, borrow so trifling a sum ten
times over from my friends, but I much prefer to make it a matter of business
and to carry out that business myself. In my position you can readily
understand that it is unwise to place one’s self under obligations.’

“‘For how long, may I ask, do you want this sum?’ I
asked.

“‘Next Monday I have a large sum due to me, and I shall then
most certainly repay what you advance, with whatever interest you think it
right to charge. But it is very essential to me that the money should be paid
at once.’

“‘I should be happy to advance it without further parley from
my own private purse,’ said I, ‘were it not that the strain would
be rather more than it could bear. If, on the other hand, I am to do it in the
name of the firm, then in justice to my partner I must insist that, even in
your case, every businesslike precaution should be taken.’

“‘I should much prefer to have it so,’ said he, raising
up a square, black morocco case which he had laid beside his chair. ‘You
have doubtless heard of the Beryl Coronet?’

“‘One of the most precious public possessions of the
empire,’ said I.

“‘Precisely.’ He opened the case, and there, imbedded
in soft, flesh-coloured velvet, lay the magnificent piece of jewellery which he
had named. ‘There are thirty-nine enormous beryls,’ said he,
‘and the price of the gold chasing is incalculable. The lowest estimate
would put the worth of the coronet at double the sum which I have asked. I am
prepared to leave it with you as my security.’

“I took the precious case into my hands and looked in some perplexity
from it to my illustrious client.
“‘You doubt its value?’ he asked.
“‘Not at all. I only doubt—’

“‘The propriety of my leaving it. You may set your mind at
rest about that. I should not dream of doing so were it not absolutely certain
that I should be able in four days to reclaim it. It is a pure matter of form.
Is the security sufficient?’
“‘Ample.’

“‘You understand, Mr. Holder, that I am giving you a strong
proof of the confidence which I have in you, founded upon all that I have heard
of you. I rely upon you not only to be discreet and to refrain from all gossip
upon the matter but, above all, to preserve this coronet with every possible
precaution because I need not say that a great public scandal would be caused
if any harm were to befall it. Any injury to it would be almost as serious as
its complete loss, for there are no beryls in the world to match these, and it
would be impossible to replace them. I leave it with you, however, with every
confidence, and I shall call for it in person on Monday morning.’

“Seeing that my client was anxious to leave, I said no more but, calling
for my cashier, I ordered him to pay over fifty £ 1000 notes. When I was alone
once more, however, with the precious case lying upon the table in front of me,
I could not but think with some misgivings of the immense responsibility which
it entailed upon me. There could be no doubt that, as it was a national
possession, a horrible scandal would ensue if any misfortune should occur to
it. I already regretted having ever consented to take charge of it. However, it
was too late to alter the matter now, so I locked it up in my private safe and
turned once more to my work.

“When evening came I felt that it would be an imprudence to leave so
precious a thing in the office behind me. Bankers’ safes had been forced
before now, and why should not mine be? If so, how terrible would be the
position in which I should find myself! I determined, therefore, that for the
next few days I would always carry the case backward and forward with me, so
that it might never be really out of my reach. With this intention, I called a
cab and drove out to my house at Streatham, carrying the jewel with me. I did
not breathe freely until I had taken it upstairs and locked it in the bureau of
my dressing-room.

“And now a word as to my household, Mr. Holmes, for I wish you to
thoroughly understand the situation. My groom and my page sleep out of the
house, and may be set aside altogether. I have three maid-servants who have
been with me a number of years and whose absolute reliability is quite above
suspicion. Another, Lucy Parr, the second waiting-maid, has only been in my
service a few months. She came with an excellent character, however, and has
always given me satisfaction. She is a very pretty girl and has attracted
admirers who have occasionally hung about the place. That is the only drawback
which we have found to her, but we believe her to be a thoroughly good girl in
every way.

“So much for the servants. My family itself is so small that it will not
take me long to describe it. I am a widower and have an only son, Arthur. He
has been a disappointment to me, Mr. Holmes—a grievous disappointment. I
have no doubt that I am myself to blame. People tell me that I have spoiled
him. Very likely I have. When my dear wife died I felt that he was all I had to
love. I could not bear to see the smile fade even for a moment from his face. I
have never denied him a wish. Perhaps it would have been better for both of us
had I been sterner, but I meant it for the best.

“It was naturally my intention that he should succeed me in my business,
but he was not of a business turn. He was wild, wayward, and, to speak the
truth, I could not trust him in the handling of large sums of money. When he
was young he became a member of an aristocratic club, and there, having
charming manners, he was soon the intimate of a number of men with long purses
and expensive habits. He learned to play heavily at cards and to squander money
on the turf, until he had again and again to come to me and implore me to give
him an advance upon his allowance, that he might settle his debts of honour. He
tried more than once to break away from the dangerous company which he was
keeping, but each time the influence of his friend, Sir George Burnwell, was
enough to draw him back again.

“And, indeed, I could not wonder that such a man as Sir George Burnwell
should gain an influence over him, for he has frequently brought him to my
house, and I have found myself that I could hardly resist the fascination of
his manner. He is older than Arthur, a man of the world to his finger-tips, one
who had been everywhere, seen everything, a brilliant talker, and a man of
great personal beauty. Yet when I think of him in cold blood, far away from the
glamour of his presence, I am convinced from his cynical speech and the look
which I have caught in his eyes that he is one who should be deeply distrusted.
So I think, and so, too, thinks my little Mary, who has a woman’s quick
insight into character.

“And now there is only she to be described. She is my niece; but when my
brother died five years ago and left her alone in the world I adopted her, and
have looked upon her ever since as my daughter. She is a sunbeam in my
house—sweet, loving, beautiful, a wonderful manager and housekeeper, yet
as tender and quiet and gentle as a woman could be. She is my right hand. I do
not know what I could do without her. In only one matter has she ever gone
against my wishes. Twice my boy has asked her to marry him, for he loves her
devotedly, but each time she has refused him. I think that if anyone could have
drawn him into the right path it would have been she, and that his marriage
might have changed his whole life; but now, alas! it is too late—forever
too late!

“Now, Mr. Holmes, you know the people who live under my roof, and I shall
continue with my miserable story.

“When we were taking coffee in the drawing-room that night after dinner,
I told Arthur and Mary my experience, and of the precious treasure which we had
under our roof, suppressing only the name of my client. Lucy Parr, who had
brought in the coffee, had, I am sure, left the room; but I cannot swear that
the door was closed. Mary and Arthur were much interested and wished to see the
famous coronet, but I thought it better not to disturb it.
“‘Where have you put it?’ asked Arthur.
“‘In my own bureau.’

“‘Well, I hope to goodness the house won’t be burgled
during the night.’ said he.
“‘It is locked up,’ I answered.

“‘Oh, any old key will fit that bureau. When I was a
youngster I have opened it myself with the key of the box-room cupboard.’

“He often had a wild way of talking, so that I thought little of what he
said. He followed me to my room, however, that night with a very grave face.

“‘Look here, dad,’ said he with his eyes cast down,
‘can you let me have £ 200?’

“‘No, I cannot!’ I answered sharply. ‘I have been
far too generous with you in money matters.’

“‘You have been very kind,’ said he, ‘but I must
have this money, or else I can never show my face inside the club again.’
“‘And a very good thing, too!’ I cried.

“‘Yes, but you would not have me leave it a dishonoured
man,’ said he. ‘I could not bear the disgrace. I must raise the
money in some way, and if you will not let me have it, then I must try other
means.’

“I was very angry, for this was the third demand during the month.
‘You shall not have a farthing from me,’ I cried, on which he bowed
and left the room without another word.

“When he was gone I unlocked my bureau, made sure that my treasure was
safe, and locked it again. Then I started to go round the house to see that all
was secure—a duty which I usually leave to Mary but which I thought it
well to perform myself that night. As I came down the stairs I saw Mary herself
at the side window of the hall, which she closed and fastened as I approached.

“‘Tell me, dad,’ said she, looking, I thought, a little
disturbed, ‘did you give Lucy, the maid, leave to go out to-night?’
“‘Certainly not.’

“‘She came in just now by the back door. I have no doubt that
she has only been to the side gate to see someone, but I think that it is
hardly safe and should be stopped.’

“‘You must speak to her in the morning, or I will if you
prefer it. Are you sure that everything is fastened?’
“‘Quite sure, dad.’

“‘Then, good-night.’ I kissed her and went up to my
bedroom again, where I was soon asleep.

“I am endeavouring to tell you everything, Mr. Holmes, which may have any
bearing upon the case, but I beg that you will question me upon any point which
I do not make clear.”
“On the contrary, your statement is singularly lucid.”

“I come to a part of my story now in which I should wish to be
particularly so. I am not a very heavy sleeper, and the anxiety in my mind
tended, no doubt, to make me even less so than usual. About two in the morning,
then, I was awakened by some sound in the house. It had ceased ere I was wide
awake, but it had left an impression behind it as though a window had gently
closed somewhere. I lay listening with all my ears. Suddenly, to my horror,
there was a distinct sound of footsteps moving softly in the next room. I
slipped out of bed, all palpitating with fear, and peeped round the corner of
my dressing-room door.

“‘Arthur!’ I screamed, ‘you villain! you thief!
How dare you touch that coronet?’

“The gas was half up, as I had left it, and my unhappy boy, dressed only
in his shirt and trousers, was standing beside the light, holding the coronet
in his hands. He appeared to be wrenching at it, or bending it with all his
strength. At my cry he dropped it from his grasp and turned as pale as death. I
snatched it up and examined it. One of the gold corners, with three of the
beryls in it, was missing.

“‘You blackguard!’ I shouted, beside myself with rage.
‘You have destroyed it! You have dishonoured me forever! Where are the
jewels which you have stolen?’
“‘Stolen!’ he cried.
“‘Yes, thief!’ I roared, shaking him by the shoulder.

“‘There are none missing. There cannot be any missing,’
said he.

“‘There are three missing. And you know where they are. Must
I call you a liar as well as a thief? Did I not see you trying to tear off
another piece?’

“‘You have called me names enough,’ said he, ‘I
will not stand it any longer. I shall not say another word about this business,
since you have chosen to insult me. I will leave your house in the morning and
make my own way in the world.’

“‘You shall leave it in the hands of the police!’ I
cried half-mad with grief and rage. ‘I shall have this matter probed to
the bottom.’

“‘You shall learn nothing from me,’ said he with a
passion such as I should not have thought was in his nature. ‘If you
choose to call the police, let the police find what they can.’

“By this time the whole house was astir, for I had raised my voice in my
anger. Mary was the first to rush into my room, and, at the sight of the
coronet and of Arthur’s face, she read the whole story and, with a
scream, fell down senseless on the ground. I sent the housemaid for the police
and put the investigation into their hands at once. When the inspector and a
constable entered the house, Arthur, who had stood sullenly with his arms
folded, asked me whether it was my intention to charge him with theft. I
answered that it had ceased to be a private matter, but had become a public
one, since the ruined coronet was national property. I was determined that the
law should have its way in everything.

“‘At least,’ said he, ‘you will not have me
arrested at once. It would be to your advantage as well as mine if I might
leave the house for five minutes.’

“‘That you may get away, or perhaps that you may conceal what
you have stolen,’ said I. And then, realising the dreadful position in
which I was placed, I implored him to remember that not only my honour but that
of one who was far greater than I was at stake; and that he threatened to raise
a scandal which would convulse the nation. He might avert it all if he would
but tell me what he had done with the three missing stones.

“‘You may as well face the matter,’ said I; ‘you
have been caught in the act, and no confession could make your guilt more
heinous. If you but make such reparation as is in your power, by telling us
where the beryls are, all shall be forgiven and forgotten.’

“‘Keep your forgiveness for those who ask for it,’ he
answered, turning away from me with a sneer. I saw that he was too hardened for
any words of mine to influence him. There was but one way for it. I called in
the inspector and gave him into custody. A search was made at once not only of
his person but of his room and of every portion of the house where he could
possibly have concealed the gems; but no trace of them could be found, nor
would the wretched boy open his mouth for all our persuasions and our threats.
This morning he was removed to a cell, and I, after going through all the
police formalities, have hurried round to you to implore you to use your skill
in unravelling the matter. The police have openly confessed that they can at
present make nothing of it. You may go to any expense which you think
necessary. I have already offered a reward of £ 1000. My God, what shall I do!
I have lost my honour, my gems, and my son in one night. Oh, what shall I
do!”

He put a hand on either side of his head and rocked himself to and fro, droning
to himself like a child whose grief has got beyond words.

Sherlock Holmes sat silent for some few minutes, with his brows knitted and his
eyes fixed upon the fire.
“Do you receive much company?” he asked.

“None save my partner with his family and an occasional friend of
Arthur’s. Sir George Burnwell has been several times lately. No one else,
I think.”
“Do you go out much in society?”

“Arthur does. Mary and I stay at home. We neither of us care for
it.”
“That is unusual in a young girl.”

“She is of a quiet nature. Besides, she is not so very young. She is
four-and-twenty.”

“This matter, from what you say, seems to have been a shock to her
also.”
“Terrible! She is even more affected than I.”
“You have neither of you any doubt as to your son’s guilt?”

“How can we have when I saw him with my own eyes with the coronet in his
hands.”

“I hardly consider that a conclusive proof. Was the remainder of the
coronet at all injured?”
“Yes, it was twisted.”

“Do you not think, then, that he might have been trying to straighten
it?”

“God bless you! You are doing what you can for him and for me. But it is
too heavy a task. What was he doing there at all? If his purpose were innocent,
why did he not say so?”

“Precisely. And if it were guilty, why did he not invent a lie? His
silence appears to me to cut both ways. There are several singular points about
the case. What did the police think of the noise which awoke you from your
sleep?”

“They considered that it might be caused by Arthur’s closing his
bedroom door.”

“A likely story! As if a man bent on felony would slam his door so as to
wake a household. What did they say, then, of the disappearance of these
gems?”

“They are still sounding the planking and probing the furniture in the
hope of finding them.”
“Have they thought of looking outside the house?”

“Yes, they have shown extraordinary energy. The whole garden has already
been minutely examined.”

“Now, my dear sir,” said Holmes, “is it not obvious to you
now that this matter really strikes very much deeper than either you or the
police were at first inclined to think? It appeared to you to be a simple case;
to me it seems exceedingly complex. Consider what is involved by your theory.
You suppose that your son came down from his bed, went, at great risk, to your
dressing-room, opened your bureau, took out your coronet, broke off by main
force a small portion of it, went off to some other place, concealed three gems
out of the thirty-nine, with such skill that nobody can find them, and then
returned with the other thirty-six into the room in which he exposed himself to
the greatest danger of being discovered. I ask you now, is such a theory
tenable?”

“But what other is there?” cried the banker with a gesture of
despair. “If his motives were innocent, why does he not explain
them?”

“It is our task to find that out,” replied Holmes; “so now,
if you please, Mr. Holder, we will set off for Streatham together, and devote
an hour to glancing a little more closely into details.”

My friend insisted upon my accompanying them in their expedition, which I was
eager enough to do, for my curiosity and sympathy were deeply stirred by the
story to which we had listened. I confess that the guilt of the banker’s
son appeared to me to be as obvious as it did to his unhappy father, but still
I had such faith in Holmes’ judgment that I felt that there must be some
grounds for hope as long as he was dissatisfied with the accepted explanation.
He hardly spoke a word the whole way out to the southern suburb, but sat with
his chin upon his breast and his hat drawn over his eyes, sunk in the deepest
thought. Our client appeared to have taken fresh heart at the little glimpse of
hope which had been presented to him, and he even broke into a desultory chat
with me over his business affairs. A short railway journey and a shorter walk
brought us to Fairbank, the modest residence of the great financier.

Fairbank was a good-sized square house of white stone, standing back a little
from the road. A double carriage-sweep, with a snow-clad lawn, stretched down
in front to two large iron gates which closed the entrance. On the right side
was a small wooden thicket, which led into a narrow path between two neat
hedges stretching from the road to the kitchen door, and forming the
tradesmen’s entrance. On the left ran a lane which led to the stables,
and was not itself within the grounds at all, being a public, though little
used, thoroughfare. Holmes left us standing at the door and walked slowly all
round the house, across the front, down the tradesmen’s path, and so
round by the garden behind into the stable lane. So long was he that Mr. Holder
and I went into the dining-room and waited by the fire until he should return.
We were sitting there in silence when the door opened and a young lady came in.
She was rather above the middle height, slim, with dark hair and eyes, which
seemed the darker against the absolute pallor of her skin. I do not think that
I have ever seen such deadly paleness in a woman’s face. Her lips, too,
were bloodless, but her eyes were flushed with crying. As she swept silently
into the room she impressed me with a greater sense of grief than the banker
had done in the morning, and it was the more striking in her as she was
evidently a woman of strong character, with immense capacity for
self-restraint. Disregarding my presence, she went straight to her uncle and
passed her hand over his head with a sweet womanly caress.

“You have given orders that Arthur should be liberated, have you not,
dad?” she asked.
“No, no, my girl, the matter must be probed to the bottom.”

“But I am so sure that he is innocent. You know what woman’s
instincts are. I know that he has done no harm and that you will be sorry for
having acted so harshly.”
“Why is he silent, then, if he is innocent?”

“Who knows? Perhaps because he was so angry that you should suspect
him.”

“How could I help suspecting him, when I actually saw him with the
coronet in his hand?”

“Oh, but he had only picked it up to look at it. Oh, do, do take my word
for it that he is innocent. Let the matter drop and say no more. It is so
dreadful to think of our dear Arthur in prison!”

“I shall never let it drop until the gems are found—never, Mary!
Your affection for Arthur blinds you as to the awful consequences to me. Far
from hushing the thing up, I have brought a gentleman down from London to
inquire more deeply into it.”
“This gentleman?” she asked, facing round to me.

“No, his friend. He wished us to leave him alone. He is round in the
stable lane now.”

“The stable lane?” She raised her dark eyebrows. “What can he
hope to find there? Ah! this, I suppose, is he. I trust, sir, that you will
succeed in proving, what I feel sure is the truth, that my cousin Arthur is
innocent of this crime.”

“I fully share your opinion, and I trust, with you, that we may prove
it,” returned Holmes, going back to the mat to knock the snow from his
shoes. “I believe I have the honour of addressing Miss Mary Holder. Might
I ask you a question or two?”
“Pray do, sir, if it may help to clear this horrible affair up.”
“You heard nothing yourself last night?”

“Nothing, until my uncle here began to speak loudly. I heard that, and I
came down.”

“You shut up the windows and doors the night before. Did you fasten all
the windows?”
“Yes.”
“Were they all fastened this morning?”
“Yes.”

“You have a maid who has a sweetheart? I think that you remarked to your
uncle last night that she had been out to see him?”

“Yes, and she was the girl who waited in the drawing-room, and who may
have heard uncle’s remarks about the coronet.”

“I see. You infer that she may have gone out to tell her sweetheart, and
that the two may have planned the robbery.”

“But what is the good of all these vague theories,” cried the
banker impatiently, “when I have told you that I saw Arthur with the
coronet in his hands?”

“Wait a little, Mr. Holder. We must come back to that. About this girl,
Miss Holder. You saw her return by the kitchen door, I presume?”

“Yes; when I went to see if the door was fastened for the night I met her
slipping in. I saw the man, too, in the gloom.”
“Do you know him?”

“Oh, yes! he is the greengrocer who brings our vegetables round. His
name is Francis Prosper.”

“He stood,” said Holmes, “to the left of the door—that
is to say, farther up the path than is necessary to reach the door?”
“Yes, he did.”
“And he is a man with a wooden leg?”

Something like fear sprang up in the young lady’s expressive black eyes.
“Why, you are like a magician,” said she. “How do you know
that?” She smiled, but there was no answering smile in Holmes’
thin, eager face.

“I should be very glad now to go upstairs,” said he. “I shall
probably wish to go over the outside of the house again. Perhaps I had better
take a look at the lower windows before I go up.”

He walked swiftly round from one to the other, pausing only at the large one
which looked from the hall onto the stable lane. This he opened and made a very
careful examination of the sill with his powerful magnifying lens. “Now
we shall go upstairs,” said he at last.

The banker’s dressing-room was a plainly furnished little chamber, with a
grey carpet, a large bureau, and a long mirror. Holmes went to the bureau first
and looked hard at the lock.
“Which key was used to open it?” he asked.

“That which my son himself indicated—that of the cupboard of the
lumber-room.”
“Have you it here?”
“That is it on the dressing-table.”
Sherlock Holmes took it up and opened the bureau.

“It is a noiseless lock,” said he. “It is no wonder that it
did not wake you. This case, I presume, contains the coronet. We must have a
look at it.” He opened the case, and taking out the diadem he laid it
upon the table. It was a magnificent specimen of the jeweller’s art, and
the thirty-six stones were the finest that I have ever seen. At one side of the
coronet was a cracked edge, where a corner holding three gems had been torn
away.

“Now, Mr. Holder,” said Holmes, “here is the corner which
corresponds to that which has been so unfortunately lost. Might I beg that you
will break it off.”

The banker recoiled in horror. “I should not dream of trying,” said
he.

“Then I will.” Holmes suddenly bent his strength upon it, but
without result. “I feel it give a little,” said he; “but,
though I am exceptionally strong in the fingers, it would take me all my time
to break it. An ordinary man could not do it. Now, what do you think would
happen if I did break it, Mr. Holder? There would be a noise like a pistol
shot. Do you tell me that all this happened within a few yards of your bed and
that you heard nothing of it?”
“I do not know what to think. It is all dark to me.”

“But perhaps it may grow lighter as we go. What do you think, Miss
Holder?”
“I confess that I still share my uncle’s perplexity.”
“Your son had no shoes or slippers on when you saw him?”
“He had nothing on save only his trousers and shirt.”

“Thank you. We have certainly been favoured with extraordinary luck
during this inquiry, and it will be entirely our own fault if we do not succeed
in clearing the matter up. With your permission, Mr. Holder, I shall now
continue my investigations outside.”

He went alone, at his own request, for he explained that any unnecessary
footmarks might make his task more difficult. For an hour or more he was at
work, returning at last with his feet heavy with snow and his features as
inscrutable as ever.

“I think that I have seen now all that there is to see, Mr.
Holder,” said he; “I can serve you best by returning to my
rooms.”
“But the gems, Mr. Holmes. Where are they?”
“I cannot tell.”

The banker wrung his hands. “I shall never see them again!” he
cried. “And my son? You give me hopes?”
“My opinion is in no way altered.”

“Then, for God’s sake, what was this dark business which was acted
in my house last night?”

“If you can call upon me at my Baker Street rooms to-morrow morning
between nine and ten I shall be happy to do what I can to make it clearer. I
understand that you give me carte blanche to act for you, provided only
that I get back the gems, and that you place no limit on the sum I may
draw.”
“I would give my fortune to have them back.”

It was obvious to me that my companion’s mind was now made up about the
case, although what his conclusions were was more than I could even dimly
imagine. Several times during our homeward journey I endeavoured to sound him
upon the point, but he always glided away to some other topic, until at last I
gave it over in despair. It was not yet three when we found ourselves in our
rooms once more. He hurried to his chamber and was down again in a few minutes
dressed as a common loafer. With his collar turned up, his shiny, seedy coat,
his red cravat, and his worn boots, he was a perfect sample of the class.

“I think that this should do,” said he, glancing into the glass
above the fireplace. “I only wish that you could come with me, Watson,
but I fear that it won’t do. I may be on the trail in this matter, or I
may be following a will-o’-the-wisp, but I shall soon know which it is. I
hope that I may be back in a few hours.” He cut a slice of beef from the
joint upon the sideboard, sandwiched it between two rounds of bread, and
thrusting this rude meal into his pocket he started off upon his expedition.

I had just finished my tea when he returned, evidently in excellent spirits,
swinging an old elastic-sided boot in his hand. He chucked it down into a
corner and helped himself to a cup of tea.

“I only looked in as I passed,” said he. “I am going right
on.”
“Where to?”

“Oh, to the other side of the West End. It may be some time before I get
back. Don’t wait up for me in case I should be late.”
“How are you getting on?”

“Oh, so so. Nothing to complain of. I have been out to Streatham since I
saw you last, but I did not call at the house. It is a very sweet little
problem, and I would not have missed it for a good deal. However, I must not
sit gossiping here, but must get these disreputable clothes off and return to
my highly respectable self.”

I could see by his manner that he had stronger reasons for satisfaction than
his words alone would imply. His eyes twinkled, and there was even a touch of
colour upon his sallow cheeks. He hastened upstairs, and a few minutes later I
heard the slam of the hall door, which told me that he was off once more upon
his congenial hunt.

I waited until midnight, but there was no sign of his return, so I retired to
my room. It was no uncommon thing for him to be away for days and nights on end
when he was hot upon a scent, so that his lateness caused me no surprise. I do
not know at what hour he came in, but when I came down to breakfast in the
morning there he was with a cup of coffee in one hand and the paper in the
other, as fresh and trim as possible.

“You will excuse my beginning without you, Watson,” said he,
“but you remember that our client has rather an early appointment this
morning.”

“Why, it is after nine now,” I answered. “I should not be
surprised if that were he. I thought I heard a ring.”

It was, indeed, our friend the financier. I was shocked by the change which had
come over him, for his face which was naturally of a broad and massive mould,
was now pinched and fallen in, while his hair seemed to me at least a shade
whiter. He entered with a weariness and lethargy which was even more painful
than his violence of the morning before, and he dropped heavily into the
armchair which I pushed forward for him.

“I do not know what I have done to be so severely tried,” said he.
“Only two days ago I was a happy and prosperous man, without a care in
the world. Now I am left to a lonely and dishonoured age. One sorrow comes
close upon the heels of another. My niece, Mary, has deserted me.”
“Deserted you?”

“Yes. Her bed this morning had not been slept in, her room was empty, and
a note for me lay upon the hall table. I had said to her last night, in sorrow
and not in anger, that if she had married my boy all might have been well with
him. Perhaps it was thoughtless of me to say so. It is to that remark that she
refers in this note:

“‘MY DEAREST UNCLE,—I feel that I have brought trouble
upon you, and that if I had acted differently this terrible misfortune might
never have occurred. I cannot, with this thought in my mind, ever again be
happy under your roof, and I feel that I must leave you forever. Do not worry
about my future, for that is provided for; and, above all, do not search for
me, for it will be fruitless labour and an ill-service to me. In life or in
death, I am ever your loving,
“‘MARY.’

“What could she mean by that note, Mr. Holmes? Do you think it points to
suicide?”

“No, no, nothing of the kind. It is perhaps the best possible solution. I
trust, Mr. Holder, that you are nearing the end of your troubles.”

“Ha! You say so! You have heard something, Mr. Holmes; you have learned
something! Where are the gems?”

“You would not think £ 1000 apiece an excessive sum for
them?”
“I would pay ten.”

“That would be unnecessary. Three thousand will cover the matter. And
there is a little reward, I fancy. Have you your cheque-book? Here is a pen.
Better make it out for £ 4000.”

With a dazed face the banker made out the required check. Holmes walked over to
his desk, took out a little triangular piece of gold with three gems in it, and
threw it down upon the table.
With a shriek of joy our client clutched it up.
“You have it!” he gasped. “I am saved! I am saved!”

The reaction of joy was as passionate as his grief had been, and he hugged his
recovered gems to his bosom.

“There is one other thing you owe, Mr. Holder,” said Sherlock
Holmes rather sternly.

“Owe!” He caught up a pen. “Name the sum, and I will pay
it.”

“No, the debt is not to me. You owe a very humble apology to that noble
lad, your son, who has carried himself in this matter as I should be proud to
see my own son do, should I ever chance to have one.”
“Then it was not Arthur who took them?”
“I told you yesterday, and I repeat to-day, that it was not.”

“You are sure of it! Then let us hurry to him at once to let him know
that the truth is known.”

“He knows it already. When I had cleared it all up I had an interview
with him, and finding that he would not tell me the story, I told it to him, on
which he had to confess that I was right and to add the very few details which
were not yet quite clear to me. Your news of this morning, however, may open
his lips.”

“For Heaven’s sake, tell me, then, what is this extraordinary
mystery!”

“I will do so, and I will show you the steps by which I reached it. And
let me say to you, first, that which it is hardest for me to say and for you to
hear: there has been an understanding between Sir George Burnwell and your
niece Mary. They have now fled together.”
“My Mary? Impossible!”

“It is unfortunately more than possible; it is certain. Neither you nor
your son knew the true character of this man when you admitted him into your
family circle. He is one of the most dangerous men in England—a ruined
gambler, an absolutely desperate villain, a man without heart or conscience.
Your niece knew nothing of such men. When he breathed his vows to her, as he
had done to a hundred before her, she flattered herself that she alone had
touched his heart. The devil knows best what he said, but at least she became
his tool and was in the habit of seeing him nearly every evening.”

“I cannot, and I will not, believe it!” cried the banker with an
ashen face.

“I will tell you, then, what occurred in your house last night. Your
niece, when you had, as she thought, gone to your room, slipped down and talked
to her lover through the window which leads into the stable lane. His footmarks
had pressed right through the snow, so long had he stood there. She told him of
the coronet. His wicked lust for gold kindled at the news, and he bent her to
his will. I have no doubt that she loved you, but there are women in whom the
love of a lover extinguishes all other loves, and I think that she must have
been one. She had hardly listened to his instructions when she saw you coming
downstairs, on which she closed the window rapidly and told you about one of
the servants’ escapade with her wooden-legged lover, which was all
perfectly true.

“Your boy, Arthur, went to bed after his interview with you but he slept
badly on account of his uneasiness about his club debts. In the middle of the
night he heard a soft tread pass his door, so he rose and, looking out, was
surprised to see his cousin walking very stealthily along the passage until she
disappeared into your dressing-room. Petrified with astonishment, the lad
slipped on some clothes and waited there in the dark to see what would come of
this strange affair. Presently she emerged from the room again, and in the
light of the passage-lamp your son saw that she carried the precious coronet in
her hands. She passed down the stairs, and he, thrilling with horror, ran along
and slipped behind the curtain near your door, whence he could see what passed
in the hall beneath. He saw her stealthily open the window, hand out the
coronet to someone in the gloom, and then closing it once more hurry back to
her room, passing quite close to where he stood hid behind the curtain.

“As long as she was on the scene he could not take any action without a
horrible exposure of the woman whom he loved. But the instant that she was gone
he realised how crushing a misfortune this would be for you, and how
all-important it was to set it right. He rushed down, just as he was, in his
bare feet, opened the window, sprang out into the snow, and ran down the lane,
where he could see a dark figure in the moonlight. Sir George Burnwell tried to
get away, but Arthur caught him, and there was a struggle between them, your
lad tugging at one side of the coronet, and his opponent at the other. In the
scuffle, your son struck Sir George and cut him over the eye. Then something
suddenly snapped, and your son, finding that he had the coronet in his hands,
rushed back, closed the window, ascended to your room, and had just observed
that the coronet had been twisted in the struggle and was endeavouring to
straighten it when you appeared upon the scene.”
“Is it possible?” gasped the banker.

“You then roused his anger by calling him names at a moment when he felt
that he had deserved your warmest thanks. He could not explain the true state
of affairs without betraying one who certainly deserved little enough
consideration at his hands. He took the more chivalrous view, however, and
preserved her secret.”

“And that was why she shrieked and fainted when she saw the
coronet,” cried Mr. Holder. “Oh, my God! what a blind fool I have
been! And his asking to be allowed to go out for five minutes! The dear fellow
wanted to see if the missing piece were at the scene of the struggle. How
cruelly I have misjudged him!”

“When I arrived at the house,” continued Holmes, “I at once
went very carefully round it to observe if there were any traces in the snow
which might help me. I knew that none had fallen since the evening before, and
also that there had been a strong frost to preserve impressions. I passed along
the tradesmen’s path, but found it all trampled down and
indistinguishable. Just beyond it, however, at the far side of the kitchen
door, a woman had stood and talked with a man, whose round impressions on one
side showed that he had a wooden leg. I could even tell that they had been
disturbed, for the woman had run back swiftly to the door, as was shown by the
deep toe and light heel marks, while Wooden-leg had waited a little, and then
had gone away. I thought at the time that this might be the maid and her
sweetheart, of whom you had already spoken to me, and inquiry showed it was so.
I passed round the garden without seeing anything more than random tracks,
which I took to be the police; but when I got into the stable lane a very long
and complex story was written in the snow in front of me.

“There was a double line of tracks of a booted man, and a second double
line which I saw with delight belonged to a man with naked feet. I was at once
convinced from what you had told me that the latter was your son. The first had
walked both ways, but the other had run swiftly, and as his tread was marked in
places over the depression of the boot, it was obvious that he had passed after
the other. I followed them up and found they led to the hall window, where
Boots had worn all the snow away while waiting. Then I walked to the other end,
which was a hundred yards or more down the lane. I saw where Boots had faced
round, where the snow was cut up as though there had been a struggle, and,
finally, where a few drops of blood had fallen, to show me that I was not
mistaken. Boots had then run down the lane, and another little smudge of blood
showed that it was he who had been hurt. When he came to the high road at the
other end, I found that the pavement had been cleared, so there was an end to
that clue.

“On entering the house, however, I examined, as you remember, the sill
and framework of the hall window with my lens, and I could at once see that
someone had passed out. I could distinguish the outline of an instep where the
wet foot had been placed in coming in. I was then beginning to be able to form
an opinion as to what had occurred. A man had waited outside the window;
someone had brought the gems; the deed had been overseen by your son; he had
pursued the thief; had struggled with him; they had each tugged at the coronet,
their united strength causing injuries which neither alone could have effected.
He had returned with the prize, but had left a fragment in the grasp of his
opponent. So far I was clear. The question now was, who was the man, and who was
it brought him the coronet?

“It is an old maxim of mine that when you have excluded the impossible,
whatever remains, however improbable, must be the truth. Now, I knew that it
was not you who had brought it down, so there only remained your niece and the
maids. But if it were the maids, why should your son allow himself to be
accused in their place? There could be no possible reason. As he loved his
cousin, however, there was an excellent explanation why he should retain her
secret—the more so as the secret was a disgraceful one. When I remembered
that you had seen her at that window, and how she had fainted on seeing the
coronet again, my conjecture became a certainty.

“And who could it be who was her confederate? A lover evidently, for who
else could outweigh the love and gratitude which she must feel to you? I knew
that you went out little, and that your circle of friends was a very limited
one. But among them was Sir George Burnwell. I had heard of him before as being
a man of evil reputation among women. It must have been he who wore those boots
and retained the missing gems. Even though he knew that Arthur had discovered
him, he might still flatter himself that he was safe, for the lad could not say
a word without compromising his own family.

“Well, your own good sense will suggest what measures I took next. I went
in the shape of a loafer to Sir George’s house, managed to pick up an
acquaintance with his valet, learned that his master had cut his head the night
before, and, finally, at the expense of six shillings, made all sure by buying
a pair of his cast-off shoes. With these I journeyed down to Streatham and saw
that they exactly fitted the tracks.”

“I saw an ill-dressed vagabond in the lane yesterday evening,” said
Mr. Holder.

“Precisely. It was I. I found that I had my man, so I came home and
changed my clothes. It was a delicate part which I had to play then, for I saw
that a prosecution must be avoided to avert scandal, and I knew that so astute
a villain would see that our hands were tied in the matter. I went and saw him.
At first, of course, he denied everything. But when I gave him every particular
that had occurred, he tried to bluster and took down a life-preserver from the
wall. I knew my man, however, and I clapped a pistol to his head before he
could strike. Then he became a little more reasonable. I told him that we would
give him a price for the stones he held—£ 1000 apiece. That brought out
the first signs of grief that he had shown. ‘Why, dash it all!’
said he, ‘I’ve let them go at six hundred for the three!’ I
soon managed to get the address of the receiver who had them, on promising him
that there would be no prosecution. Off I set to him, and after much chaffering
I got our stones at £ 1000 apiece. Then I looked in upon your son, told him
that all was right, and eventually got to my bed about two o’clock, after
what I may call a really hard day’s work.”

“A day which has saved England from a great public scandal,” said
the banker, rising. “Sir, I cannot find words to thank you, but you shall
not find me ungrateful for what you have done. Your skill has indeed exceeded
all that I have heard of it. And now I must fly to my dear boy to apologise to
him for the wrong which I have done him. As to what you tell me of poor Mary,
it goes to my very heart. Not even your skill can inform me where she is
now.”

“I think that we may safely say,” returned Holmes, “that she
is wherever Sir George Burnwell is. It is equally certain, too, that whatever
her sins are, they will soon receive a more than sufficient punishment.”

十一.
绿玉皇冠奇案
「福尔摩斯，」一日清晨我立于我们那扇凸窗前望着街上说道，「来了一位疯子。他亲属竟容他独自出门，未免可悲。」
我朋友懒洋洋地从扶手椅上起身，双手插在睡袍的口袋里，越过我肩望去。这是个明朗清冽的二月早晨，前一日的雪仍厚厚铺在地上，在冬阳里闪着耀眼的光。贝克街中央那一带已被往来车马轧成一条褐色脆碎的带，可两侧与人行道边堆起的雪埂仍如初降之时般洁白。灰色的人行道已被清扫刮净，可仍滑得险，故行人比往常稀少。事实上从大都会车站方向走来的，唯有这位行止怪异、引起我注意的绅士。
他约莫五十岁，身材高大富态、气宇轩昂，一张厚实而轮廓鲜明的脸，体态有威严之相。他衣装沉郁却不失华贵——黑色礼服，闪亮的礼帽，整洁的褐色脚套，剪裁得体的珍珠灰长裤。然而他的举动却与他衣冠风貌的庄严相形见绌——他正使劲地奔跑着，时而还做几下小跳，恰如一个不大锻炼、又被迫赶路的疲乏之人。他奔跑时把双手忽上忽下地甩动，头颅左右晃，脸上扭出种种古怪非常的表情。
「他究竟出了什么事？」我问。「他在抬头看街旁房屋的门牌呢。」
「我看他正是来此处，」福尔摩斯搓着手说。
「来此处？」
「是；我倒以为他是来求我办公事。我看我已识其征兆。哈！我所言不假罢？」他话音未落，那人便气喘吁吁地冲到我们门前，把门铃拉得满屋哐当作响。
几秒钟后他便已在我们屋里——仍喘着，仍指手画脚——而那双眼里凝着如此固执的悲苦与绝望，我们的微笑顷刻间化为惊骇与怜悯。他一时说不出话，只是身子摇晃着，把头发一把一把抓乱，恰如一个被逼至理智极限的人。继而他骤然立起，将头猛撞向墙壁，我们俩急忙冲上去把他拽至屋中央。夏洛克·福尔摩斯把他按入扶手椅中，自己挨他坐下，轻拍他的手，以他善用的那种轻柔抚慰的声调与他闲聊起来。
「您是来向我倾诉故事的，是不？」他说道。「您因匆忙而疲乏。请等您自己稍稍恢复，然后凡您所托付之难题，我无不愿尽心查察。」
那人坐了一会儿，胸膛起伏，与情绪奋力搏斗。继而他用手帕拂过额头，紧抿双唇，把脸转向我们。
「您必以为我疯了？」他说道。
「我看您是遇上了大麻烦，」福尔摩斯答。
「天知道我遇上了！——一桩足以令我神志失据之难——这般突如其来，又这般可怕。声誉之耻我或可承当——虽我之品节素来未曾沾染过半分污点。私事之忧亦人人皆有；可二者并至，又以这般可怕之形——足以使我灵魂为之颤动。何况，并非只我一人受难。倘此可怖之事不得脱解，国中至贵之人亦将受累。」
「请您安心，先生，」福尔摩斯说，「请您把您是何人、又遭遇了何事，清楚地告诉我。」
「敝人之名，」我们的访客答道，「您耳中想必并不陌生。我便是亚历山大·霍尔德——针线街上霍尔德与史蒂文森银行的合伙人。」
这名字我们确实熟知，他乃是伦敦城中第二大私营银行之资深合伙人。那么，究竟是何事，竟将伦敦的一位首屈一指的市民逼至这般可怜之境？我们带着十足的好奇心等候。终于，他又奋力一振，开始讲述。
「我深感时间宝贵，」他说，「故警长一建议我请教您，我便急忙赶来。我乘地铁到贝克街，从那里步行赶来——因为这场雪里马车走得太慢。这便是我何以喘成这样——我素来甚少运动。如今好些了，我便尽量简短而清楚地把事实陈给您听。
「您当然知道，一个成功的银行业务，既要靠拓展往来与储户之数，亦要靠为我们的资金寻得能生息的投资。我们最赚钱的一项放款方式，便是以无可挑剔之担保品作抵押。近年来我们在此一面颇有作为，许多贵族家庭都曾以其名画、藏书或银器作抵向我们贷出大笔款项。
「昨日上午我正坐在银行办公室中，一名职员递进一张名片来。我一看那名字便惊起——竟是——好罢，纵向您也只能道：那是一个全球皆知的名字——英国最高、最贵、最尊崇之名之一。我对这一份荣幸不胜其惊；他进屋时我正欲表达，他便径直入正题——那神态像一个想尽快办完不愉快之事的人。
「『霍尔德先生，』他说，『我所闻您惯于放款。』
「『敝行在担保品稳妥时是放的，』我答。
「『我必须立刻得到五万英镑，』他说，『这区区数额我自然可向友人借十遍而有余，可我极愿把这事作为公事办，且由我自己来办。以我的位置，您当能体谅，使自身落入人情之债是不智的。』
「『请问您要借多久？』
「『下周一我将有一大笔款项进账，届时必偿还您所借出之款，连您认为合理收取之息一并付清。但金额必须立即支付，这一点对我极为紧要。』
「『我本可不再多议，从我私人财产中拨与您，』我说，『可那将令我一时承受不住。倘我以敝行名义借出，则出于对合伙人之公正，便是您这般客户，我亦须坚持采取一切商业上的稳妥措置。』
「『我倒更愿如此，』他说，从座位旁举起一只方形黑色摩洛哥皮匣。『您必听过绿玉皇冠之名罢？』
「『国朝最珍贵的公共宝物之一，』我答。
「『正是。』他打开匣子，匣内嵌于柔软的肉色丝绒之中的，正是他所提之名的那件辉煌珠宝。『其上有三十九颗硕大绿玉，』他说，『金匠雕刻之价值更不可估算。最低估计：本冠之值是您所要借款之倍。我愿留此作我之担保品。』
「我把这珍贵的匣子接在手中，从中抬头望向我这位显赫的客人，颇有几分困惑。
「『您怀疑其价值？』他问。
「『决不。我只怀疑——』
「『——把它留下是否合宜？这点您可放心。倘非确信我四日内必能赎回，我决不敢动此念。这只是一道形式。担保品足够否？』
「『绰绰有余。』
「『您应明白，霍尔德先生，我把它留与您，便是给了您一份基于您之名望的极强之信任。我倚靠您不仅守口如瓶、不论及此事，更且——以一切可能之方式——保全此冠。我无须多言：倘其有任何损伤，便将引起轩然大波。任何损伤，几乎与全失同等严重，因举世再无与此匹配之绿玉，无可替补。然而我以全然之信赖把它留与您；周一上午我将亲自来取。』
「见我的客人急于离去，我便不再多言，唤来出纳吩咐他付出五十张面值一千英镑之钞票。可我独自一人时，那珍贵的匣子摆在面前的桌上，我却忍不住怀着隐忧想到这件巨大的责任。无可置疑，这是国宝；倘有不测，必引起可怕的丑闻。我已悔自己应承下此任。可事已至此，无从更改，我便把它锁入私保险柜，又转向手头的工作。
「至傍晚，我觉得把这般珍贵之物留在身后办公处实属不智。银行之保险柜从前亦曾被撬，敝行之柜何以独不能？倘真发生，我所处境地将何等可怕！故我决意：往后几日，我将随身把这匣子带来带去，决不让它真正脱离我手。怀此意，我唤了一辆马车，把这珠宝带回我斯特里塞姆的家中。直至我把它带到楼上，锁入更衣室的写字台，我方才舒一口气。
「关于我的家中诸人，福尔摩斯先生，请容我交代清楚——我望您能彻底明了情形。我家的马夫与小厮都不在屋内夜宿，可不必计较。我有三名女仆，已在我家多年，其忠诚可信全然无疑。还有一名露西·帕尔，二等女仆，入我之差仅数月。然而她带来的人品荐书极佳，向来令我满意。她长得很俊俏，吸引了几个仰慕者，时不时在屋外徘徊。这是我们对她唯一所发现之缺憾；可我们仍信她是个各方面皆好的姑娘。
「仆人便说到这里。我家本身极小，须不了多少话便能描述。我是个鳏夫，唯有一子，名叫亚瑟。福尔摩斯先生，他于我是一桩失望——一桩深切的失望。我无疑要自责。人皆道我宠坏了他，恐确是如此。爱妻去世时，我觉得他便是我所有可爱的一切，连他脸上微笑稍一褪去都不忍见。我从未拒绝过他任何一个心愿。或许待他更严些，我们父子两人皆将更好——可我之心意是为了他好。
「我之本意自然是要他承袭我之事业，可他并非做生意的料子。他放浪、任性，老实说我也不敢让他经手大宗钱款。他年轻时入了一家贵族俱乐部，又因举止迷人，不久便与几个手头宽裕、习性奢侈的人相交甚密。他染上了豪赌，又在跑马场上挥金如土，以至于一次次回来求我预支他的零用钱以清偿那些『荣誉之债』。他不止一次试图脱离他所交的危险之伴，可每一次他朋友乔治·伯恩韦尔爵士的影响都足以把他拉了回去。
「实在，乔治·伯恩韦尔爵士这般人能令他倾心，并不为奇——他多次随他到我家来，连我自己都觉得他那份魅力难以抗拒。他比亚瑟年长，举止周到圆通，是位见多识广、四海行走的人，谈吐熠熠，相貌出众。然而我冷静下来——离开他那份令人晕眩的临场之魅——我便由他玩世不恭的言谈与我曾捕捉到的他眼中的神情确信：此人极不可信。我如此想，我那小玛丽亦如此想——她有女子那种敏锐的看人之直觉。

「现在便只剩她要描述了。她是我的侄女；可五年前我兄弟过世，把她孤零零地丢在世上，我便收她为养女，自此便视她如亲女。她是我家中的一缕阳光——温柔、可爱、美丽，又是出色的管家与持家者，亦如女子所能温柔、安静、体贴。她是我的右手，没有她不知我能做什么。仅有一事她曾忤过我的意。我那男孩两次向她求婚——他爱她至深——可她两次都拒绝了。我以为，倘有人能把他引上正路，必是她；他若结了这门婚事，整个人生或将改观。可如今——唉！太迟了——永远太迟了！
「福尔摩斯先生，我屋顶下住的诸人您已知矣，我便接着说我那可悲的故事。
「那夜晚饭后我们正在客厅中喝咖啡。我把今日的经历与我们屋顶下的珍宝说与亚瑟与玛丽听——只略去客人之名。露西·帕尔送咖啡进来后，我看见她已离屋；可门是否关上我无法确证。玛丽与亚瑟兴致颇浓，欲一睹这件名冠，可我以为不宜动它。
「『您把它放在哪里？』亚瑟问。
「『在我自己的写字台里。』
「『天哪，但愿夜里屋子莫遭贼。』他说道。
「『锁着呢，』我答。
「『噢，那写字台用什么旧钥匙都开得开。我小时便用储物间柜子的钥匙开过它呢。』
「他常胡言乱语，故我也不甚在意。可那夜他随我至我屋，神情却极沉重。
「『爸爸，您看，』他低着眼睛说，『可否让我支二百英镑？』
「『不可！』我厉声答道。『钱事上我对您实在已宽容过分了。』
「『您一向极慈，』他说，『可这钱我必须有，否则我便再也无颜进俱乐部之门。』
「『不进也好！』我喝道。
「『您总不能让我作为蒙耻之人离开吧，』他说，『这羞辱我无法承当。我必须设法筹得这笔钱；若您不肯给，我便另谋他法。』
「我极是愤怒——这已是月内第三次伸手要钱了。『从我这里您得不到一个铜板！』我喝道。他便鞠了一躬，一语未发离了屋。
「他走后我开锁查看，确认我的宝物仍安然，又锁好。然后我去查看屋内是否门窗皆牢——这本是玛丽的份内之事，可那夜我以为还是亲自查一遍为妥。我下楼时见玛丽正在前厅边的窗户旁——我走近时她正合上栓闩。
「『爸爸，告诉我，』她说道，神色我看略有几分不安，『今夜您可允了女仆露西出门？』
「『决然未允。』
「『她方才才从后门进来。我相信她不过是去后门见个什么人，可这恐怕不甚安全，须加以制止。』
「『明早您与她说，或您愿，由我说。门窗皆已锁牢罢？』
「『十分确定，爸爸。』
「『那便晚安。』我吻了她，又上楼回房，不久便已入睡。
「我尽量把可能与本案有关之事都告诉您，福尔摩斯先生；倘我有所未明之处，恳请您随时发问。」
「正相反，您所述清晰非常。」
「我现在要讲到的一段，我尤希望讲得分外清楚。我并非沉睡之人；那夜心中之忧无疑令我比平日更不沉。约凌晨二时，屋中某种声响把我惊醒。等我完全清醒时声响已止，可它留下的印象，恍如某处窗户被轻轻关上。我躺着，凝神倾听。忽然——令我惊骇——分明有脚步声在隔壁房中轻轻移动。我心如鹿撞地溜下床，从更衣室门角探头窥视。
「『亚瑟！』我尖叫，『您这恶徒！您这窃贼！您怎敢动那皇冠？』
「煤气灯如我所留半亮。我那不幸的男孩只穿着衬衫与长裤，立在灯光旁，手中捧着皇冠。他似在使劲地拧它，或竭尽全力地把它折弯。听到我之喊，他失手把它落了，脸色苍白如死。我抢起来一看，金冠的一角连同其上三颗绿玉，已不见了。
「『您这无赖！』我怒不可遏地喝道。『您把它毁了！您让我永世蒙耻！您偷的那几颗宝石呢？』
「『偷？』他叫道。
「『是，窃贼！』我吼着，揪住他的肩。
「『没有少。不可能少。』他说。
「『少了三颗。您知它们在何处。我除了称您为窃贼，难道还得再叫您骗子？我刚才不是分明看见您在试图掰下另一片么？』
「『您骂得已经够多了，』他说，『我不愿再忍。既您选择如此辱我，我便对此事一字不再说。我明早便离开您家，自己去闯天下。』
「『您将被警察带走！』我半疯了一般大叫。『此事我必查个水落石出。』
「『您从我口中休想得知一字，』他答道，那激愤的神情我未曾料到他天性之中竟有。『您要叫警察，便让警察去查吧。』
「至此，整宅已被我之怒声惊动。玛丽是头一个冲入我屋的，一见皇冠与亚瑟之脸，便已读出全貌——尖叫一声，昏倒在地。我吩咐女仆去叫警察，立即把调查交到他们手中。督察与一名巡警入屋时，亚瑟一直阴沉地双臂交叉立着，问我是否要以盗窃罪指控他。我答此事已不再是私事，而是公事——因被毁的皇冠是国宝。我决意一切皆按律行事。
「『至少，』他说，『您不至要我立即被捕。可否容我离屋五分钟——这对您和我皆有利。』
「『您是要逃走？还是要藏起您所窃之物？』我说。继而我意识到自己所处之可怕境地，恳请他记得：此事所赌不仅是我的名誉，更是某位远比我更尊贵之人的名誉；他正要掀起一场震动全国之丑闻。倘他肯把那三颗失踪宝石之下落告诉我，便可避免这一切。
「『您还是面对这局面罢，』我说。『您是当场被擒；任何招供都不会令您之罪更可恨。倘您肯尽您所能补救——告诉我们绿玉在何处——一切便可既往不咎。』

「『把您的宽恕留与那些请求宽恕之人，』他答道，对我冷笑着转过身去。我看出他已心硬如石，我之言无能动他。只剩一途。我把督察唤入，把他交给警方羁押。当即对他本人、其房间，以及屋内任何他可能藏宝之处进行了搜查；可未能寻得宝石之踪迹，纵然我们如何劝诱、威胁，那不幸的男孩亦不肯启口。今晨他被押入囚室；而我办完一切警务手续之后，便急忙赶来求您，恳请您动用您的本领来解开此案。警察已坦言眼下他们一筹莫展。您以为必要之处，开支可任凭。我已悬赏一千英镑。我的天，我该如何是好！我一夜之间失去了名誉、宝石，与儿子。噢，我该如何是好！」
他双手按住头之两侧，前后摇晃，自言自语地哀吟着——如一位悲伤已超出言语的孩子。
夏洛克·福尔摩斯沉默端坐数分钟，眉头紧锁，目光凝在炉火之上。
「您府上常有客来么？」他问。
「除我合伙人与他家眷，及偶来的亚瑟之友，别无他人。乔治·伯恩韦尔爵士近来来过几次。再无他人，我看。」
「您常出入应酬么？」
「亚瑟常出入。我和玛丽留家。我们都不喜应酬。」
「这在年轻女子之中倒不寻常。」
「她性子安静。何况她也不算很年轻——已二十四岁了。」
「依您所言，此事于她想必亦是冲击。」
「极大的冲击！她比我还要更受影响。」
「您二位皆未曾对令郎之罪有所怀疑？」
「我亲眼见他手持皇冠，怎能不疑？」
「我倒不以为这是确凿之证。皇冠的其余部分可有损坏？」
「是，扭曲了。」
「那您不以为他是在试图把它扳直么？」
「上苍庇佑您！您正在为他、也为我尽心。可这负担太重了。他在那里干什么？倘其意无辜，何以不直说？」
「正是。倘有罪，又何以不撒一谎？他之沉默于我看来两面通用。本案中颇有几桩奇异之处。警方对令您醒来的那一阵声响有何看法？」
「他们以为或许是亚瑟关上卧室门所致。」
「真是可信！仿佛一个意图行窃之人会甩门到惊动全宅。那么对宝石失踪一事他们又怎么说？」
「他们仍在叩地板、戳家具，希望寻见。」
「可曾想过往屋外去找？」
「想过，他们办事极卖力。整片花园已被仔细搜过。」
「亲爱的先生，」福尔摩斯说道，「您难道未察觉，此事实远比您与警方起初所以为的更深？您看似一桩简单的案子，于我看来则极为复杂。请想想您之假设含有什么。您假设令郎自床上下来，冒着大险，进入您的更衣室，开了您的写字台，取出皇冠，使尽蛮力把它的一小块掰下，去到别处，把三十九颗中的三颗藏起——藏得无人能寻；然后又带着其余三十六颗回到他被发现之险最大的屋中。我请问您，这般假设可立得住么？」
「可还能有别的什么？」银行家以绝望之态喊道。「倘他动机无辜，何以不解释？」
「那便是我们要查的，」福尔摩斯答。「霍尔德先生，请，眼下我们一同前往斯特里塞姆，再花一个钟头细看一番。」

我朋友坚要我同行，我也乐意得很——这故事所引起我之好奇与同情极深。我承认，那位银行家之子之罪在我看来一如他不幸的父亲所看那般明显；可我对福尔摩斯的判断有如此之信赖，故我以为只要他对所谓之解释不满，便仍可怀有希望之根据。一路向南郊去时他几乎一语未发，下颌抵胸，礼帽压低过眼，沉入最深之沉思。我们的客人则因方才那一线希望而似乎又振了精神，甚至开口与我闲话他业务之事。一段短短的火车，再加更短的步行，便把我们带到了「美宁镇」——这位大金融家朴素的居所「公平岸」。

「公平岸」是一栋宽大的方形白石宅邸，与街道隔了几步。前面是双向之马车道，覆雪的草坪沿之而下，至两扇大铁门把入口闭合。右侧有一小片木林，引向两道修剪整齐的篱间小径，自街通至厨房门——便是商贩出入之径。左侧则有一巷，引向马厩，本身并不在宅院之内，乃是公共而少人行走之通道。福尔摩斯把我们留在门口，自己缓步绕宅而行——前廊、商贩之径、绕到屋后花园，再到马厩巷。他去了好一会儿，霍尔德先生与我便进了餐厅，靠炉火等他归来。我们正默坐时，门开，一位年轻女士走了进来。她身材略高于中等，纤瘦，黑发黑眼——这眼眸在她那绝白的肤色衬托下更显幽深。我以为我从未见过女子脸上有这般令人心惊的苍白。她的嘴唇亦无血色，可眼里却因哭过而泛红。她默然走入屋时，给我的悲伤之印象比晨间银行家所给的还要深；又因她显然是位性格坚强、有极强自制之力的女子，这印象便愈发动人。她不顾我之在场，径直走向叔父，以一种甜柔的女子的爱抚把手抚过他头。
「爸爸，您已下令把亚瑟放出来了，是不？」她问。
「不，不，我的孩子，此事必查个水落石出。」
「可我如此确信他无辜。您知女子之直觉是怎样的。我知他未做坏事——您将为您这般苛厉而后悔。」
「他若无辜，何以不语？」
「谁知道呢？或许因您怀疑他，他过于愤怒。」
「我亲眼见他手持皇冠，又怎能不怀疑他？」
「噢，可他不过是拾起来看看。噢，请，请，听我之言，他无辜。请放手吧，莫再说了。一想到我们亲爱的亚瑟在牢狱里，我便心痛！」
「在宝石找到之前我决不放手——决不，玛丽！您对亚瑟之爱使您看不见我所将面临的可怕后果。我不仅没有压下此事，反而从伦敦请来了一位绅士，再深入查察。」
「便是这位绅士？」她转向我问道。
「不，是他朋友。他要我们让他独自查察。他此刻在马厩巷那边。」
「马厩巷？」她扬起黑眉。「他在那里能指望寻到什么？啊！这位想必便是他了。先生，我盼您能证明——我深信便是真相——我堂兄亚瑟与此罪无涉。」
「敝人完全赞同您之看法，亦盼能与您一同证之，」福尔摩斯一面说，一面退回门垫上把鞋上之雪拍掉。「我有幸是在向玛丽·霍尔德小姐说话么？容我问一两个问题罢？」
「请问，先生，倘有助于澄清此可怕之事。」
「您昨夜可曾听见什么？」
「未——直到我叔父在此处大声说话之时。我听见了，便下了楼。」
「您前夜关好了门窗。所有窗子可都拴好了？」
「都拴好了。」
「今晨它们可仍都拴着？」
「都拴着。」
「您家有一个女仆有相好的人？昨夜您似对您叔父说她已出门去见他了？」
「是，她便是那个在客厅伺候过咖啡、可能听到了叔父谈论皇冠的姑娘。」
「我明白。您的推断是：她或出门告知了相好的人，二人或共谋了这桩盗窃。」
「这般含糊的揣测有何用？」银行家不耐烦地嚷道。「我已告诉您：我亲眼见亚瑟手持皇冠！」
「霍尔德先生，请稍候。我们必将回到这一点。霍尔德小姐，关于这位姑娘，您是看见她从厨房门返回的？」
「是；我去查看夜里门是否拴牢时撞见她正悄悄进来。我亦看见暗影中那男人。」
「您可识他？」
「噢，识！便是给我们送菜来的菜贩，名叫弗朗西斯·普罗斯珀。」
「他立的位置，」福尔摩斯说，「在门之左侧——也就是说，比走到门所必经之处更朝小径之里？」
「是，他立在那里。」
「他还是个装木腿之人？」
那位年轻女士那双富有表情的黑眼里掠过几分类似惊惧之色。「您简直像个法师，」她说。「您是怎么知道的？」她笑了，可福尔摩斯那张瘦削而急切的脸上未见回笑。
「我现在很乐意上楼去，」他说。「我大概还要再绕屋外查察一遍。也许在上楼之前先看看一楼的窗子为好。」
他急步从一扇窗到另一扇，唯独在门厅那扇朝马厩巷的大窗前停了下来。他把它打开，用他强力的放大镜极仔细地查窗台。「现在我们上楼罢，」他终于说道。
银行家的更衣室是一间陈设朴素的小屋，一张灰色地毯，一张大写字台，一面长镜。福尔摩斯先到写字台前，盯着锁看了好一阵。
「是用哪一把钥匙开的？」他问。
「便是我儿自己所言的那一把——储物间柜子的钥匙。」
「那钥匙在此？」
「梳妆台上便是。」
夏洛克·福尔摩斯把它拿起，开了写字台。
「这是把无声之锁，」他说。「难怪未把您惊醒。这只匣子，我猜便装着皇冠。我们须细看一下。」他打开匣子，取出冠戴放在桌上。这是一件珠宝匠艺之绝品，那三十六颗宝石是我此生所见之最佳。冠之一侧有一处崩裂的边缘——三颗宝石所在的那一角已被掰下。
「霍尔德先生，」福尔摩斯说，「这便是与那不幸丢失的一角相对应的一角。请您把它掰断罢？」
银行家惊骇地后退。「我可不敢。」他说。
「那我来。」福尔摩斯倏然使劲——可未能成功。「我能感觉它略有让步，」他说，「可纵然我手指力气异常之大，亦得花上好一会儿才能掰下。寻常之人决不可能。霍尔德先生，倘我真把它掰下，您以为会怎样？必有手枪般的爆响。您要告诉我：这一切发生在距您床数码之处，您却毫无察觉？」
「我不知该作何想。这一切于我皆是黑暗。」
「可往下走或会渐明。霍尔德小姐，您怎么想？」
「老实说，我仍与叔父一般困惑。」
「您看见他时，令郎是没有穿鞋或拖鞋的？」
「他只穿着长裤与衬衫。」
「多谢。这场调查中我们幸运得不寻常；倘最后未能厘清此事，全是我们自己的过失。霍尔德先生，请允我现在出去，把外面的查察接着进行。」
他自请独行——他解释道：任何不必要的足印都将使他之差更难。他工作了一个钟头有余，最后归来时，足上压着雪，神色一如既往不可窥测。
「霍尔德先生，我想我已看见此处一切可看之物，」他说，「我能为您效劳的最佳之策便是返回我之住处。」
「可宝石呢，福尔摩斯先生？它们何在？」
「此刻我无法奉告。」
银行家绞着双手。「我将再也见不到它们了！」他叫道。「我儿呢？您可给我希望？」
「我之看法毫无更改。」
「那么——看在上苍份上——昨夜我家里上演的究竟是何等阴森之事？」
「明早九时至十时之间，您可来贝克街我之住处，届时我将乐意尽力把它说得更清楚些。我所知您给了我全权代您行事，唯一条件是把宝石追回，您对我可动用之款不设上限？」
「我愿倾家荡产以换它们回来。」
「极好。我自此至明早将就此事调查。再会；今晚之前我或须再来此处一次。」
我看得出我同伴此时已就案情心有定见，至于他的结论是何，我连模糊的猜想都没有。归途中我数次试图就这一点向他探问，可他总滑到别的话题上去，最后我只得绝望地放弃。我们再次回到住处时尚不到三点。他急忙进屋，几分钟便又下来——已扮成一个寻常的混混。竖起的衣领，那件油亮褴褛的外套，红色领巾，磨损的靴子——他便是这一阶层的完美样本。
「我看这便差不多了，」他瞧了瞧壁炉上方的镜子说道。「华生，我只盼您能与我同行，可恐怕不便。我或已上了正轨，亦或在追一缕鬼火，可不久我便能知是哪一种。我盼数小时内即能回来。」他从橱柜上的一块烤肉上切下一片，夹在两片面包之间，把这粗糙的一餐塞入口袋，便启程去了。
我刚喝完茶，他便回来了，显然兴致极佳，手中晃着一只旧弹力侧筒靴。他把它丢到屋角，自己倒了一杯茶。
「我只是路过看一眼，」他说。「我马上就走。」
「去哪里？」
「噢，到西区另一边去。我可能要好一会儿才回来。倘我晚归，您不必候我。」
「您进展如何？」
「噢，马马虎虎。无可怨之处。我自上次见您之后又去过斯特里塞姆，可未到府上。这是个极可爱的小问题，我决不愿错过。可我不能在这里闲谈，须脱下这身不像样的衣服，回到我那十分体面的本来面目去。」
我看他的神态便知，他满意之根据远不止他口头所言。他眼里含光，连那病黄之颊上都泛起一抹血色。他匆匆上楼，几分钟后我听见前门一声砰然——便知他又出去追他那心头爱的猎物了。
我等到午夜，他仍未归来，便回房去了。他在追案时连日连夜在外不归本是常事，故他之晚归并不教我惊讶。我不知他是几点回来的，可我清晨下楼用早餐时，他便已在那里——一手执咖啡，一手执报，面色焕然、衣冠整齐之至。
「华生，请您原谅我没等您便先开始了，」他说，「您当记得我们的客人今早约得颇早。」
「咦，已过九点了，」我答道。「若来者便是他，我亦不奇怪。我似乎已听见铃响。」
果然便是我们的金融家朋友。我见到他的变化大为吃惊——他原本宽阔厚重的脸如今凹瘪下来，发也至少白了一调。他进屋时那副疲惫倦怠之相比昨晨那狂躁之态还要令人心痛；我推过去的扶手椅，他重重地跌坐入。
「我不知我做了什么以致受此严重之试炼，」他说。「两日之前我还是个幸福而兴旺之人，世上无忧无虑。今我却被丢与孤独蒙耻之晚景。一忧紧接一忧而至。我侄女玛丽弃我而去了。」
「弃您？」
「是。她今晨之床未曾睡过，房中空空，门厅桌上有一封她留我之信。我昨夜伤心而非愠怒地对她说，倘她肯嫁我儿，他或可一切如初。或许我说这话太轻率了。她在信中提到的便是这句话：
「『最亲爱的叔父：我觉得我给您带来了麻烦；倘我当初行事不同，这桩可怕的不幸或本不会发生。心中怀此一念，我再不能在您屋顶下安然欢愉，我觉得必须永远离开您。莫为我之将来担忧——这一节已有着落。最重要的是，请勿寻我——徒劳无功，且于我无益。无论生死，我永远是您的爱侄，
「她这字句究竟是何意，福尔摩斯先生？您看是否暗指自尽？」
「不，不，决无此意。这或许便是最妙的解决。霍尔德先生，我相信您之磨难已近终局了。」
「哈！您这般说？您必听到了什么，福尔摩斯先生；您必查到了什么！宝石何在？」
「您不会以为每颗一千英镑算太贵罢？」
「我愿付十倍。」
「不必。三千英镑便足以了断此事。我想还另应有一点酬金。您可有支票簿？这是笔。开成四千英镑罢。」
银行家茫然写下所求之支票。福尔摩斯走到自己写字台前，取出一小块嵌着三颗宝石的三角形金片，扔在桌上。
我们的客人欢呼一声把它紧紧抓起。
「您找到了！」他喘道。「我得救了！我得救了！」
他这一阵欢喜之激烈，与方才之悲苦相映。他把寻回的宝石抱在胸前。
「霍尔德先生，您还欠一桩，」夏洛克·福尔摩斯颇为严肃地说。
「欠？」他抓起笔来。「请说数额，我这便付。」
「不，所欠并非于我。您欠那位高贵少年——您之子——一份谦卑之歉。他在此事中之自处，倘我有日有子，我必以他为楷范而骄傲。」
「这么说不是亚瑟拿了它们？」
「我昨日告诉过您，今日再说一遍：不是。」
「您确信！那我们立刻去见他，把真相已大白告诉他！」
「他已知矣。我把一切厘清后便见过他，发现他不肯告诉我故事，便由我告诉他——他这才不得不承认我说得对，并补充上几条我尚不甚清楚的小细节。今晨您之消息，则或可使他更敞口而言。」
「看在天份上，请您告诉我，这桩奇事究竟是何谜？」
「我便讲，并把我达到此论的步骤一一示您。请容我先说出最难启齿之言、亦最难听之言：乔治·伯恩韦尔爵士与您侄女玛丽之间早有默契。他们如今已私奔。」
「我的玛丽？决不可能！」
「不幸乃远不止『可能』——而是『确凿』。您与令郎皆未能识破此人之真面便把他迎入您家圈内。他乃英国最危险之人之一——一个倾家荡产的赌徒，一个绝境中的恶徒，一个无心无良之人。您侄女对此种人毫无所知。当他向她吐着对她许下的誓言——他在她之前已对一百人许过——她竟自喜以为唯有自己触动了他之心。这魔鬼究竟说了什么唯他自知；至少，她已成了他的工具，惯于几乎每晚与他相会。」
「我不能、也决不肯相信！」银行家面色灰败地叫道。

「那我便告诉您昨夜您家中所发生之事。您侄女在她以为您已上楼之时，便溜下来，从那扇通向马厩巷的窗与她的情人交谈。他的足印深深压入雪中——可见他在那里立得颇久。她把皇冠之事告诉了他。他对金子之邪欲一闻此言便燃起，便把她屈服于其意。我毫不怀疑她爱您；但有些女子，恋人之爱便扑灭一切别种之爱——我看她必是其一。她还未听完他之指令，便见您下楼，便迅速合窗，又把方才那桩女仆与她木腿恋人的小风波告诉您——这一节是完全属实的。

「您之子亚瑟与您面谈之后便上床了，可因俱乐部之债而焦虑，未能酣睡。半夜他听见门外有轻足步过，便起身张望，惊见他堂妹极隐秘地沿走廊而行，走入您之更衣室。这少年惊得呆若木鸡，套上几件衣裳，便在暗中候着，看这桩怪事将如何收场。不久她便又自屋中出来，借走廊那一盏灯之光，您之子见她手中竟捧着那珍贵的皇冠。她下了楼；他心头一阵恐惧，奔过去躲在您门旁的窗帘后，从那里可俯瞰下方门厅之事。他见她偷偷开了窗，把皇冠递给暗影中某人，然后又关上窗，急忙回到她房里——经过他所躲的那帷幕之处近在咫尺。

「她在场时，他不能有任何动作，否则便要把所爱之人公诸于世。可她一离开，他便立时觉悟到这将给您带来怎样毁灭性之打击，又何等紧要必将其纠正。他便径直地——光着脚——冲下楼去，开了窗，跃入雪中，沿巷奔去——在月光下他可见一暗影。乔治·伯恩韦尔爵士试图逃走，可亚瑟把他拉住，二人扭打起来，您的少年抓着皇冠一头，他对手抓着另一头。在扭打中您之子击中乔治爵士的眼上方，把他打伤。然后某物突然咔嚓一断，您之子发现皇冠已落入他手，便奔回，关上窗，上至您之屋；正注意到皇冠在扭打中已变形，正在尽力扳直之时，您出现了。」
「这可能么？」银行家喘道。
「您随即怒骂他——而那一刻他正觉得自己应得您最热忱之谢。他不能解释真相，否则便要出卖一个本不太值得他在意之人。他却选择了更骑士般之道，守住了她的秘密。」
「这便是她见到皇冠时尖叫昏倒之故，」霍尔德先生叫道。「噢，我的天！我何等盲目愚蠢！还有他求出去五分钟之事——亲爱的孩子是想看看那丢失之块是否落在扭打之处。我何等残忍地误解了他！」

「我到您府上时，」福尔摩斯接着道，「立即极仔细地绕宅一圈，看雪中是否有可助我之痕。我知昨晚以后未再降雪，又知曾有重霜以保印迹。我沿商贩之径走，可印迹皆被踩乱不可辨。可仅过此径，在厨房门远侧，曾有一女与一男立此交谈过——男子一侧之圆形印迹表明他装的是木腿。我甚至能看出他们曾被惊扰，因女子是急促奔回门去——脚尖印深、脚跟印浅；而木腿则候了一会儿，才走开。我当时便想：这或便是您先前提及的女仆与她的相好——一问，果然如此。我绕过花园未见别的什么，只有杂乱之印——我以为是警察之印；可一进入马厩巷，雪中便写出一段又长又复杂的故事于我面前。

「有两道靴印之双行，又有第二组双行——令我惊喜——属于一个赤足之人。从您所告，我立即确信赤足者便是您之子。第一组靴印是来回皆走，第二组则疾奔；又因他的足印在某些处覆于靴印之凹陷上，可见他是后来过的。我顺迹追之，发现它们引至门厅之窗——那靴主在等候时已把雪磨得殆尽。我又走至另一端——百码或更远的巷尾。我看见靴主转过身去，雪被踩得如有过扭打的样子，最后看见几滴血落下——告诉我我所推不误。靴主继而沿巷奔去，又有一抹小小的血迹——说明受伤者乃是他。当他到那一头大路上，我发现路面已被清扫，故那条线索便至此为止。
「然而进入屋内后，您当记得，我用放大镜查察了门厅那扇窗的窗台与框架，立时便能看出有人由此出去。一只湿足踏入时所留的足背轮廓清晰可辨。我便开始能就所发生之事形成意见。一人在窗外候着；某人把宝石递出；这一事被您之子所目睹；他追上窃贼；与之扭打；二人各扯皇冠一端，合力造成单凭其一皆做不到的损伤。他带着战利品回去，可一片落入了对手之手。至此我已分明。眼下的问题是：这个人是谁？又是谁把皇冠递到他手中？
「我有一句老格言：当您把不可能之事尽数排除之后，所余的——纵然如何不可信——必是真相。我知不是您把它递下去的，故只剩您侄女与女仆。可若是女仆，您之子何以肯让自己代她受冤？决无可能之理由。然而既他爱他堂妹，则他守住她的秘密便有极妙之解释——尤其这秘密之可耻。再当我想起您见过她在窗前、且她再见皇冠时晕倒——我之猜测便成了确信。
「那么她的同谋是谁？显然是位情人——除此之外有谁能压过她对您所怀之爱与感激？我所知您甚少出门，您交友圈也极有限。其中便有乔治·伯恩韦尔爵士。我此前便闻其名——是位在女子中名声极坏的人。穿那双靴子、留下失踪宝石的必是他。即便他知亚瑟已发现了他，他仍可自以为安然无恙——因这少年但开口一言便要把自家牵入。
「至于我下一步采取之措，您之常识自能想见。我扮作一个混混到乔治爵士府上，与他贴身仆人套上交情，得知他主人前夜砍破了头；最后以六先令之代价，买下他一双弃下之鞋——便万事可证了。我带这双鞋下到斯特里塞姆，一看，恰与那些足印相合。」
「我昨晚在巷里见过一个衣装狼狈的流浪汉，」霍尔德先生说。

「正是。便是我。我得知我已找到了我的人，便回家换了衣服。我此时所演之角色颇为微妙——因我知必须避免起诉以避丑闻，我又知这般狡狯之徒会看出我们手上掣肘。我便去见了他。起初他自然否认一切。可当我把所发生之事一一道来，他便要虚张声势，从墙上取下一柄护身的棍。可我熟知他，他还未挥下，我便把一支手枪抵到了他头上。他这才稍稍讲点理。我对他说，我们将出价买他所握之宝——每颗一千英镑。这才头一次见他露出悲色。『真该死！』他说，『我已三颗六百卖出去了！』我答应他不予起诉，便从他口中得知收赃者之地址。我立即起身赶去——一番讨价还价后，以每颗一千英镑得回了我们的宝石。然后我去探望您之子，告诉他一切已成；最后约莫凌晨两点回床——可说是真正辛劳的一日。」
「这是把英国从一桩巨大公众丑闻中救出的一日，」银行家起身说道。「先生，我言语难尽我之谢；然您将不会发现我对您之所为忘恩。您之本领实远超我所闻。如今我须急赴爱子之处，向他为我所作之冤而道歉。至于您所告我之可怜玛丽，刺入我心。即您之本领亦无能告我她此刻何在。」
「我以为我们可稳妥地说，」福尔摩斯答道，「她在乔治·伯恩韦尔爵士所在之处。同样可定的是，她无论犯下何等罪过，皆将不久便受到远超其罪之惩罚。」

8.title: VIII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE SPECKLED BAND
source_paragraphs:
VIII.
THE ADVENTURE OF THE SPECKLED BAND

On glancing over my
notes of the seventy odd cases in which I have during the last eight years
studied the methods of my friend Sherlock Holmes, I find many tragic, some
comic, a large number merely strange, but none commonplace; for, working as he
did rather for the love of his art than for the acquirement of wealth, he
refused to associate himself with any investigation which did not tend towards
the unusual, and even the fantastic. Of all these varied cases, however, I
cannot recall any which presented more singular features than that which was
associated with the well-known Surrey family of the Roylotts of Stoke Moran.
The events in question occurred in the early days of my association with
Holmes, when we were sharing rooms as bachelors in Baker Street. It is possible
that I might have placed them upon record before, but a promise of secrecy was
made at the time, from which I have only been freed during the last month by
the untimely death of the lady to whom the pledge was given. It is perhaps as
well that the facts should now come to light, for I have reasons to know that
there are widespread rumours as to the death of Dr. Grimesby Roylott which tend
to make the matter even more terrible than the truth.

It was early in April in the year ’83 that I woke one morning to find
Sherlock Holmes standing, fully dressed, by the side of my bed. He was a late
riser, as a rule, and as the clock on the mantelpiece showed me that it was
only a quarter-past seven, I blinked up at him in some surprise, and perhaps
